The ancient people did not think of the pos

they naturally sought out the most durable
materials possible for their records. The
thoughts of the Egyptians were recorded on
stone, the Assyrians impressed their records
upon tablets of clay and the Greeks and
Romans used ivory, metals, or wood.


When wood came into use for the engraving
of records, new word came into the English
language through the name of the close
grained beechwood on which our Teutonic fore
fathers wrote their accounts, letters, and calen-
dars This wood was plentiful in northern
Europe, and was generally used for the pur-
pose Of preserving records


The Anglo-Saxon name for the beech was
.'boc," the Danish 'beuke' and the German
'buche," 50 it is easy to see the derivation OF
our own book.

NEW YORK, December 17-Hun-
dreds of detectives passed an automobile
parked 25 feet from the entrance to
police headquarters yesterday without
discovering that it contained the body
of an eX-conv1ct trussed up in burlap
bag.


The car had been reported stolen "a
hours earlier.


After the car had stood for four hours
In front of headquarters without arous-
ing suspicion. member of the bomb
squad looked inside and prodded the
bundle.


The bag was ripped open in the pres
ence of hundreds of officers, and the
victim was identified as Joseph
"Washie" Weskefsky


His hands were tied behind his back
with stout cord. his knees were buc-
kled to his chest, and the cord was
twisted tightly around his neck. This is
the procedure which has been followed
in several sack murders" recently.


Police files showed Weskefsky had
been convicted twice of burglary Mrs.
Weskefsky said she last saw her hus-
band at $50 O'Clock Thursday night.


When police found handbills i'll the
car advertising reduction in dry clean
ing prices, they said the killing may
have been the outgrowth of racketeer-
ing trouble in the cleaning and dyeing
industry.

sustained by Mrs Connor July year
ago while en- route to the Rapidan with

The suits, fled in the District Su-

part of the driver of motor bus which

nandale and Fairfax, Va.

space to Connor's car after being
warned. and that the bus collided with

Hearn represented the plaintiffs.


The accident, which occurred July
10, 1881, revived agitation for a police
escort for White House cars. Accord
ing to newspaper accounts, the bus
fell into line between the presidential
limousine and that of secret service
men following It, . The secret service
car and one automobile containing
newspaper correspondents succeeded in
passing the bus, which was headed the
same direction as the presidential
party, but Connor met with disaster in
the attempt.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


DANVILLE, Va. August 25.-Henry
County authorities continued their
search for two men who attacked and
robbed William Metz, filling station
owner, and burned his filling station.


He had been aroused about 3 am
yesterday by the pair, in a car bearing
North Carolina tags, who wanted to
purchase some gasoline. While MAX
ing chance, he was suddenly black
lacked, given ether and left Tor dead
in the filling station. which the robbers
set fire before speeding away.


Metz regained consciousness in time
to drag himself out of the burning
structure, which was completely de-
stroyed His son, at home nearby. was
attracted by the flames and found MIN
on the ground behind the burning
building. Metz could not say how much
money he had left in the cash register
the night before.

The rising river, swept by a high
wind from the east, Tapped over the
sea wall in East Potomac Park yester-
day and last night, depositing sea
weed along the Speedway.


The wind, which was recorded at
more than 40 miles an hour at the
airport, broke eff several trees on Hams
Point and broke five or six small boats
from their moorings In Washington
Channel. Harbor police captured the
drifting launches during the evening
and park police stood ready to close
East Potomac Park as the water threat
ened to rise over the sea wall and in
undate the point.


The fords in Rock Creek Park were
closed as the creek rose, but little DAM
age was reported in any Of the parks
save for few broken trees and some
debris which must be cleaned away.


Rainfall I'll Inches.


The Weather Bureau said 2.71 inches
of rain fell in the city during the four
days since the rain started early
Sunday.


At high tide last night the Eastern
Branch crept over roadways in Ana
costa Park. necessitating the closing
OF roadWays between Pennsylvania ave-
nue. and Anacostia Bridges.


With the high-pressure area and
cooler temperatures that today brought,
however, the rain ceased, and the river
was almost back to normal The brisk
northwest breeze which followed the
high east winds Of yesterday had al
most died down at noon, and fair"
conditions again prevailed.


May Rain Tomorrow.


The fair weather will continue
through today and early tomorrow. the
Weather Bureau predicted, but another
disturbance is due to bring rain again
late tomorrow and overnight. Late Sat-
urday, however. is due to bring another
clear period. which will probably con-
tinue over the week end with low tenn
peratures


Weather Bureau forecasters said the
lowest temperatures of the season prob
ably will come either late Saturday or
sometime Sunday, possibly below the
freezing mark

Special Dispatch to The Star


BALTIMORE, Nd. November 10
With more than $4,000 damage to
small ships and waterfront property al
ready reported Baltimore was prepared
today for a renewal of the 55-mile-an-
hour gale which, with spasmodic rain,
halted water and air traffic last night.


The entire feet Of vessels belonging
to the Maryland Yacht Club was
threatened, several small piers washed
away and the boardwalk at the club
covered by rising water Numerous pri-
Vately owned craft were sunk, one man
being blown from the deck Of his boat
into the swirling waters.


Steamers scheduled for clearing de-
layed their departure Ferry boats,
barges- dredges and other commercial
ships were forced to put back to their
piers or seek safe harbors. Part of the
quarantine stations wharf at Leading
Point was washed away.


The storm seemed to center around
the bay area, with damage to nearly
all beach resorts and fishing COM
munities


The Washington Weather Bureau
warned that tropical storm from the
Bahamas was moving northeastward
and might be accompanied by shifting
gales and winds Of hurricane force in
this vicinity today,

BOISE, Idaho September 28.-Al-
though her condition remains serious,
Mrs. William E. Borah, stricken II days
ago with parrot fever, continued an ap-
parently successful battle against the
disease today.


On the basis Of the latest bulletins
Issued by her physician, she was growing
stronger and a weakened heart condi-
tion, which had caused alarm, was I'M
proving.


The wife Of the United States Senator
yesterday asked for solid food for the
first time in several days, but physicians
deemed it best she should have liquid.

Borah recognized her husband and
spoke to him briefly yesterday. He has
been at her bedside almost constantly,
during the day, since her illness.

day night To escort the yachts into

treads.

cars equipped with machine guns and in

function Of calvalry, in mopping up and
pursuit.

mOtOrlZaClOn mas prOOuceC Qluerent

summed up his impressions by declar-
ing that motorization functioned in pro-
portion to its distance from the actual
firing line, the closer one got to the line
the more difficulties it had to face.


Camouf1age was highly developed
during the maneuvers and so well were
the troops hidden that frequently OBJ
servers had difficulty in finding them.
Joseph Paul -Boncour, minister Of war.

camouf1aging ability of the troops which

NIAGARA FALLS, N. Y, March 81
Caught in the swift currents of the
upper Niagara River late last night
hundreds of wild swans were swept over
the Horse Shoe and American Fails,
many being killed and others wounded
The lower river today was filled with
lead and wounded swans, and river men
were preparing to rescue the wounded
birds, if possible.


The swans, numbering more than 500,
river men estimated, settled on the
upper river yesterday afternoon. A
strong wind blowing upstream pre-
vented them from being carried down
stream, but as night fell the wind di-
minished and the birds were caught in
the river currents and carried over the
2 ice foes, falling with the water,
swept many of the birds against the
upper section of an ice bridge" that
formed in the gorge and the birds were
caught in the ice. Observers on shore
counted more than $50 dead birds, fast
in the ice. Others, injured by being
dashed against the rocks on their trip
over the falls, crawled o- flew to the
foes and remained huddled in small
groups. Many suffered broken legs and
wings in their descent of the waterfalls.

From the Philadelphia Public Ledger.


Two thousand people who lost their
lives in Cuba in last weeks hurricane
are the latest Of many thousands who
have, ever since man first knew the
Caribbean Islands, been periodically
sacrificed to the storms that brew at
sea, come swirling in between North
and South America and lay waste those
lands nestled beside the Gulf Stream.
Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Santo Do
mingo, Haiti and even the Florida main
land have all felt that fury and seen
their homes destroyed, their fields
devastated and their people left dead
or dying. 1t is the old, old story of
wind and torrential rain striking at
lands that are forever recovering and
never safe.


Both Haiti and Puerto Rico have
often felt the blow. Last year Puerto
Rico felt it again. The year before that
Haiti was particularly hard hit. Four
years ago Puerto Rico was strewn with
ruin, and Cuba as well was left battered
and in mourning. In 1926 an eSpe-
cially violent storm roared through the
Caribbean and struck the mainland in
Florida with terrific fury. Other years
have seen such storms whip across the
blue waters and go whirling even up
the Mississippi Valley.


It Is q storm center of the Western
World, and the plight of its people
comes directly from the hurricane.
Whether its storms are bred in the
sWirling ocean currents, in the trade
winds or in the distant upper atmos-
phere, the result is the same-death,
devastation and constant battles with
q merciless storm god.

NEW YORK, June 1.-The stock
market today showed alternate strengrn
and weakness and closed with prices
mixed


AT the opening, pronounced strength
prevailed, with gains in active issues
running up to 5 points and more. This
was succeeded in the early afternoon
by fresh wave Of liquidation, cancel
ing practically all of the early gains
and bringing many stocks down to new
low ground. Finally, in the last hour,
prices hardened and the close was at
irregular net changes.


The reason for the early strength was.
Of course, the Senates tax vote That
brought heavy short covering. For the
midsession selling no adequate explana-
ton was offered. 1t was said that bank
loans were being closed out. But that
was conjecture. Probably the new tax
on power output had something to co
with the selling in the utilities. which
were acutely weak. Electric power out
put was down again this week, but the
comparison was vitiated b. the inclu-
sion of the Memorial day holiday.

cialy convincing, was ascribed to the
announcement of the Young Commit
tees plans for supporting the bond
market


During the course of the day bear

ican Telephone. Consolidated Gas. Pub
lie Service of New Jersey. General Mo-
tors. Pennsylvania Railroad and United
States Steel common


The market was strong all around at

where from TO and more points, with
the largest gains in issues which had

that the ticker was unable to keep up

initial rush to buy. however. the pace
sla, kened

hour We're American Can. up over
points, American Telephone up almost
3, AtchiSOn up almost and General
Foods up to points. The strength
was not confined 10 any one group. On
the reaction tobacco and merchandising
shaAs were specially sensitive Wool
worth came down easily and so did
American Tobacco B The setback
took in nearly all stocks which had been
so buOyant earlier in the session.


The markets movement was entirely
normal, considering its position. After
a period Of undiluted pessimism, the
first rebound coming on favorable out
SIDE developments is Invariably followed
by profit taking and tentative new short
selling. which cancels a large part Of
the initial advance The real test comes
on this reaction. If the lower prices are
taken advantage Of by new buyers, the
indications are that a real turn has
come. The market today was at this

At least another month beyond April
/ will elapse before the new Hugh M.
Browne Junior High School can be
opened as the result of the flooding
of the buildings basement through the
bursting of a water main Sunday, ii
was learned at the Franklin School

Workmen from the Water Depart
ment and the District Repair Shop are
endeavoring to clear the silt ana muo
from the equipment that was buried IN

Among the most expensive items
which were submerged were series
of motors used to operate the ventilat-
ing and the vacuum cleaning system
for the building. The electric trans
formers which control the lighting
systems also constitute items of expen-
sive equipment which were damaged
Besides these the cafeteria tables ano
chairs, the kitchen stoves and mechan-
ical devices, including dishWashers
and several hundred students lockers
were buried beneath the slime


Flood Second Reason.


The food constitutes the second rea-





much needed school, which is located
on Twenty-fourth street northeast,
overlooking the Anacostia River, north
of Benning road.


The building apparently was COM
pleted in January, In time for Its orig
inally scheduled opening date OF Feb
ruary l.. It's staff of teachers and Of
ficers was appointed. Discovery Of the
settling of the cateterias concrete floor,
however. necessitated close inspection
of the buildings foundations, which, It
was feared, were settling in the clay on
which the building was erected. Fol-
lowing several days examination and
the subsequent relaying of section of
the cafeteria floor, the building was
pronounced fit. However, the neces-
sary walks had not been completed and
the municipal architects office, through
S B. Walsh, assistant municipal archi-
tect, announced that the structure
would not be ready for occupancy be-
fore April 1.


Garnet c.. Wilkinson, first assistant
superintendent of schools, said today
the school may not be use dthis term

set up for February opening date, is
scattered in i've northeast elementary
schools. The 663 Students thus accomo-
dated today are responsible for 20 part
time classes at the Burville, II at

Cause of Water Probed.


Investigation of the building this
morning revealed the course which the
water from the broken main took in
entering the building. Jere j. Crane,
school business manager, explained The
iron 10-inch water main snapped off
4 feet from the southern end wall. The
tremendous volume of water thus re-
leased tore up great gullies in the clay
fill about the building, followed the
foundation wall to its footings, tun-
neled beneath them. and rose in an
earth floored, unfinished basement
chamber.


The rising waters in this chamber
broke the door leading into the base
ment corridor. The water then forced
open the doors into the cafeteria, ris-
ing to a height of 4 feet


The catastrophe was further height
ened by the fact that the clay fill in
front of the building was indiscrim-
inately dumped on the manhole hous-
ing the main shutof valve, so that
time was lost in futile hunt for this
means of shutting off the flood. The
water finally was turned off at the
valve on Benning road, quarter mile
away.

The well known monkey suits" of
the Army Air Corps are about to be
relegated to the past.


The monkey suit" was the one-piece
heavy Winter flying garment which was
supposed to keep out the chill Of the
upper air. Many and many an Army
pilot, however, cursed with chattertng
teeth monkey suits, which failed Ia
mentally to keep their hapless wearers
warm.

long research work, a new two-piece
suit which has been tested and accepted
as standard and which will gradually
replace the old equipment until the
last of the old monkey suits has become
nothing more than a museum piece.

CALDWELL, Ohio, May 18.-Binding
four bank officials and seven customers
with rope. three hold-up men escaped
today with $4,000 from the Noble
County National Bank here. They
looted the cashiers cage, the vault and
the pockets of their victims.


Entering the bank the robbers
menaced the officials and customers
with pistols, herded them into the presi-
dents office and bound them with the
rope they carried. They then searched
the victims and took all valuables.


A systematic search OF the vault and
cashiers cage followed and all currency
was removed. The safety deposit boxes
were not disturbed.


Noble County officials said the rob-
bers devoted from to 10 minutes to
the search for money and they walked
to a waiting automobile in which they
fed toward Marietta.

TIENTSIN. China, January 15.-Chi-

we're surrounded and practically an

The small vegetable garden becomes
Of special interest this year. Even in
a city backyard one can raise some
vegetables sufficient for small family.
A plot 20 feet by 40 feet should give
ample returns for a small family, and
a 10 by IS foot plot, if kept constantly
at work, will produce for family plenty
of small vegetables, such as beets, car
rots, radishes, lettuce and the like.


One may raise on small plot more
vegetables in proportion than on
larger area, because of the ease with
which one may carry on the work.


Do not choose, in a small backyard,
vegetables that require too much room,
such as corn, pole beans, peas and
cabbage Concentrate on bush beans,
tomatoes, beets. carrots. lettuce and
New Zealand spinach. Onion sets may

returns.

lowing varieties are excellent:

mignonette, Clark. seeded, tennis ball;
spinach, New Zealand, excellent for

Lucullus; kohlrabi. early white Vienna;
radish, early scarlet globe.


Beans should not be planted until
about May 10. Tomato plants, egg
plants, peppers and celery can 60 out
early in June, for these should either
have been started long ago from seed
indoors or you must buy the plants.


The best way to plant a vegetable
garden is in straight rows. Radish,
lettuce, beets, Swiss chard and carrots

often one plants altogether too many
plants in a given space, with the result
that they crowd badly and injure one
another. Also landscape gardeners tell
us that broken line of plants is more
desirable than solid planting The
taller growing species naturally should
be placed at the back.


Too often the soil close to the foun-

dug. 1t is hopeless to expect plants to
thrive in this stiff clay, so that it be-

Of the old soil and to replace it with

grandif1ora also makes an attractive

ester, are too tall and soon outgrow their

houses.


As humble substitute for shrub

NEW YORK, July 21.-With the rail-
road shares as the leaders in the first
part Of the session and the oils taking
the same place in the second half, to-
days stock market forged slowly ahead
to a new high on the present recovery.


Except in a few preferred stocks

ton OF prices on the tape was very
impressive. In the stocks showing ac-
t1vity the advance was uniform and
maintained to the end, with the high
prices made in the last hour. Among
the features we're the buying in Union
Pacific, said to be for foreign account
and the new high for the year in At
lantic Refining.


Tobacco stocks, food shares, mining
issues and various specialties we're in
demand at intervals. The utilities were
neglected and standard industrials,
while slightly higher, did not figure as
prominently as usual. 1t was a market
in which the advance depended upon
new leaders


For the strength in the rails the
commonly accepted explanation was the
determination of the executives, as re-
vealed in their published statements,
to restrict competition among them
selves. There may have been other
reasons, but they were not apparent
The buying was deliberate and origi-
mated in the preferred issues which
gave 1t the semblance of investment
accumulation


The two preferred stocks most promi-
nent were Atchison and Union Pacific.

the latter more than three points during
the first two hours. Both still gave
extraordinarily high yields, Atchison
more than 10 per cent and the Union

recent lows.


OF the common stocks, Union Pacific

& Hudson, Norfolk g. Western and
Louisville & Nashville, the last ordi-
narily very inactive. Buying in Louis
Vile & Nashville the Street heard, was
for financial institutions.


Industrials were irregular through
out the forenoon, but never weak. This
was true of the standard issues such
as Allied Chemical, American Can and
United States Steel Speculation for
the rise concerned itself with special
ties. Vulcan Detinning was bid up.
International Cement advanced on thu
higher prices for the commodity. Con-
tinental Baking preferred was in de-
mand a point or so higher. American
Sugar preferred jumped over 8 points,
again illustrating the search for high
yielding investment issues.


While the market acted we'll. it failed
to convince the large bear interest still
with short contracts outstanding. They
argued that there WIS no justification
for higher prices in the trade outlook.
They belittled the statement of the rail-
way executives. They viewed with
alarm" the developments in Germany,
although the bend market seemed to
have recovered from its fright. They
pointed to the continued depressi in
commodities. instancing whe=t and cot
ton. The answer was that the market
had taken all these things into account
and had Decided that the price level

LAYING brilliant tennis in a
- drizzling rain, Frank
/ Shields and Ellsworth Vines


turned back the Canadians
in the last two battles of the
Davis Cup series yesterday at the
Chevy Chase Club, to give the
United States clean sweep of all
five matches.

trim Marcel Rainville in straight

Dominion ace, DR.. Jack Wright,
S-6, 81, 80, 6-1.

New Orleans about two weeks hence
with clean slate


The contest with Canada was already
won when the players took the court
today, as a smashing doubles victory
yesterday, following two singles triumphs
Thursday, had clinched the series.


But the tall, young Americans were
out to win, and the outcome of neither
match was never seriously In doubt, al
though in each set Vines had to come
from behind.


Shields made better scores against the
dapper Canadian, DR.. Wright, than
Vines had made on Thursday, when he
was forced to go five sets.


Both Yanks Erratic.


Both Vines and Shields occasionally
1apsed into errors and seemed not ye.
to have reached their best form, although
noticeaoly improved over their recent
play


The first principle Of tennis-to get
the ball over the net-gaye Vines less
trouble than it did in his match with
Wright.


Rainville played q steady game and
fought stubbornly but Vines shots had
a zip and an agile that the Canadians
could not match.


The Californians sharp-shooting was
deadly as he ran the French Canadian
from one side Of the court to the other.


Rainville won the first three games OF
the first set, the first two of the second
set and three of the first four games
Of the third set. But each time, Vines,
when pressed, turned on the steam and
sent his drives and smsShes whistlins
into the corners for decisive points that
carried him ahead.


Shields Service Strong.


Shields, whose play 80 far this sea-
son has been below par, was substituted
for Wilmer Allison, so that he could show
whether he was approaching his past
form. He appeared to have regatned
control Of his service and in the final
set burned in seven aces, four in one
game.


Shields often went to the net for
volleying attack, but the canny Wright
countered in the third set with a series
of beautiful lobs. This broke up the
New Workers. volleying temporarily and
enabled Wright to take the set. The
Canadian champion played at top form,
his drives giving Shields plenty Of trou-
Bile. but he could not hold the hard
hitting American with his crushing
service.

SAC PAULO, Brazil, March 16
GN.SO.-Trappers and others
familiar with Brazil's vast jungleS
today conjectured upon the possi-
bility that Col. P. H. Fawcett,
British explorer, still was alive
after having been out of touch
with civilization for almost seven
years.


Hopes that the explorer still
lives were revived with the report
of trapper to the British consul
general, Arthur Abbott, that he
had met a white man, bearded
and dressed in skins, who claimed
to be Fawcett.


There were the possibilities
that if the man we're Fawcett, he
was being held captive.


Although several expeditions
have set out to find the explorer,
no definite word has been re-
ceived of him since he departed
for the interior with his 21-year.
old son, Jack, and another young
Englishman, Raleigh Rimell, in
1925.

PORTIONS.


Have liver cut in about two

substitute fat Add onion for the

then add the sliced pepper, from

removed. Add tomatoes mixed

well. When well blended add
chilli powder, reduce heat very
low and simmer gently until

an hour. Then add cooked peas
and the rice. Stir together gently
and serve hot. Diced pieces of
leftover liver could be used. In

together about 20 minutes, then

starch, fat, fiber. Rich in cop

with Speaker Garner on the ticket

HONOLULU, August 1.-Searching

Waianae Mountains today seeking four
officers and three enlisted men missing
since Friday on a reconnaissance detail


No word has been received from the
party since it left Shofield Barracks
The missing men are Maj. Joseph Va
chon, Capts. George S. Pierce, Arthur
K. Noble and William F. Stevenson;
Sergts. Cristmore and Andrews and Pvt
Johnston. all of the 18th Infantry.


The party had carried pigeons, but

barracks. Land parties and an airplane
are participating in the search.


The party carried rations for several
days. Army officials are not alarmed
because Of the small area covered by
the forests, and believe the men will
soon find their way out If they are lost.

night. If she ever said prayers

O he.

world. No doubt she often
thought of the manner in

Mexico.

market looked tired and prices we're bid
up with effort on the part of the spon-
sors for the various leaders, but the re-
suit was achieved. The close was higher

During the morning the leaders were

stocks. In the late afternoon the motors
we're taken up, with ChrySler and Cen
eral Motors beth turned over in large

ders appeared and the market began

PERNAMBUCO, Brazil (P).-With
the purpose of further reducing the
importation of gasoline, the state gov
ernment here has decided that motor
lists using alcohol or other fuel pro-
duced locally shall have reduction OF
10 per cent in auto taxes over car
owners who use gasoline pure.


For some time there has been an
increasing use Of alcohol made here
from sugarcane, especially in heavy
trucks.


The federal government at Rio de
Janeiro several months ago decreed
that oil companies must dilute gasoline
with per cent Brazilian alcohol before
marketing it, and the large importing
companies, like Standard Oil, have been
obliged to pay for this amount of alco-
hol with every importation. But
sufficient supply of alcohol has not
been available so no mixing has been
done.

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, April IL
P).-The town of Mendoza, terrified by
two-day rain Of volcanic ash from the
Andes, rejoiced today as the manifesto
tion stopped and the sun shone through
for the first time since Sunday


Government officials, who had pre-
pared to evacuate the city's inhabitants,
reconsidered, for it appeared the dan
ger was over.


Ashes lay more than IA inches deep
over some of the territory. Earlier wes-
teTly winds showered the fine dust down
In a fanlike belt 800 miles across
Central South America.


Await First Aid.


Ofhcials here had considered re-
quests for railway facilities to begin the
evacuation of Mendoza and other af-
flicted areas should the situation grow
worse. Half dozen villages near Men
doZa, which was shaken three times
yesterday, awaited the arrival of gov
ernment trucks bearing first aid sup
plies to the people, many of whom have
been without sleep for two night, terri
fed by the rain of ashes and the sui
phurous gases.


Volcanoes were becoming active which
have long been considered dead. At
Mdidl suc SdI11 CIdChS appeared laSt
night and the ash blanket was 1875
inches deep before midnight.


In spite Of the widespread terror
throughout the western territory, more
conservative scientists here were in
clined to believe that the volcanic ac-
tivity was more frightening and dis
commoding than actually dangerous.


Many Towns Dark.


The superintendent of telegraphs in
the Mendoza district telegraphed the
minister Of interior early this morning
that darkness, ash clouds and gases
overhung the towns of Chilecto. San
Carlos, La Consulta, Campo Los Andes.
San Rafael and Tunuyan yesterday.
From these foothill towns the 80o-mile
fan of ash showers extended across
South America at midnight, enveloping
BuenoS Aires, Montevideo, most Of Uru-
quay and even the ships along the At
lsntic seacoast in a grayish cloak.


The shower here was OF an almost in
visible powder, but it continued into
its second day, and left a thorough
coating over streets and roofs like snow.
Reports from San Rafael said breath
ing was difficult there and the rum
blings continued, with bright flashes in
the direction of the Andes. The min
istry Of interior was asked to rush
drums Of oxygen for treatment of cases
of asphyxiation from the gases. A
cavalry detachment went to the aid of
the most severely stricken villages.


Cattle in Danger.


Many towns throughout the country
burned street lights yesterday Busi-
ness houses at Trenque La Quen, an
important town 300 miles southwest Of
here, closed because of the ashes and
darkness. The snowy drift here
whitened clothing and stung the eyes
and its gritty substance filtered into
Offices and homes.


Railroads reported most trains from
the west delayed on, account Of poor
visibility. Argentine farmers rejoiced
over the free fertilization for their lands
from the nitrates in the dust, but this
was offset by the danger to stock from
the dust-covered grasses.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


BURLINGTON, VT, September "a
The upset in the supposedly rock-ribbed
State of Maine has given the Repub-
lican leaders in Vermont much food for
thought and through the newspapers
they are calling on the State. county
and town committees to get busy and
start an energetic campaign.


The fact that the Democrats had only
one candidate for each of the principal
State Offices at the primary last week
while the Republicans were divided and
the further fact that the Democrats are
apparently united in their views about
national issues. particularly prohibition,
while the Republicans are far from
agreement on the latter question. leads
many to believe that the vote for Roose-
welt in November will far exceed that
ever cast in the Green Mountain State
for any Democratic nominee for the
Presidency.


Roosevelt's visit to the State early in
the month enthused Vermont Demo-
Gratis to a point not reached in many
years, but if Calvin Coolidge could be
induced to attend rally at Montpelier
and appeal for votes for Hoover. Yer
mont Republicans might show some OF
the enthusiasm which now prevails
among their political opponents.

BY the Associated Press.


SHANGHAI, August 1.-The death
toll was counted at 500 as the rampag-
ing Chu Kiang Canton River which
has been battering down the huts in
the poorer districts of this southern
capital Of China continued to rise
today.


Heavy rains in the various river
basins in the Canton area last week
started the rise. The situation grew
alarming last Saturday as houses start
ed collapsing A home for the aged
was undermined and 80 persons
perished beneath the debris


Many fires were started by torn lines
and from other causes. 1t was esti-
mated 600 houses had collapsed.


Dispatches from other parts Of China
indicated torrential rains had fallen in
Western ShenSi and the Yellow River
had broken its dykes, inundating 80
towns and leaving $4,000 homeless.


(Advices from the north in Man
churia today said tens of millions of
dollars had been the damage of tor
rental rains and floods around
Kailiang. A food shortage for the Win
ter was threatened)

BY the Associated Press.


NEW YORK, September l9-Business
ard industrial mag gazine editcrs through
out the country, reporting trade trends
during the early part Of this month
to the Associated Business Papers, Inc,
observed a slow upward movement in
many lines.


1t was reported building contracts in
creased substantially; Midsummer ad-
vances in cement prices were holding
steady; carloadings showed a better
than seasonal rise; credit was more
readily available for railway improve
ments, and labor troubles showed a
tendency to decrease.


Pig iron demand and ingot produc-
tion were found to be rising somewhat
slowly, while machinery orders were a
trif1e ahead Of July; oil producers and
rcfiners were Sowing down production,
customary to this period; chemical con-
sumption continued to rise. while the
country's stocks were declining; the
paint trade exhibited improved demand
from both industrial and consumer
sources; woodworking plants were doing
moderately better, but millwork build
ing continued low.


The editcrs especially stressed the
improvement in the textile industry.
Cotton stocks, it was said. were the
lowest on record, with untitled orders
the highest since March, 1929. Whole
sale dry goods buying was found to be
heavy stores apparently stocking against
rising commodity prices.


Printers reported increasing requests
for estimates, particularly in the large
Eastern cities. The hotel business
showed some improvement and meat
packers stated that consumption was
maintaining a normal level.

LEBANON, Tenn, Sept. 6
(I.N.S.). - After threatening
to storm the Jail here, despite
the presence of National
Guardsmen with machine guns,
a mob Of 500 farmers was dis
persed today by news that the
five negro prisoners they
sought had been transferred to
Nashville prison.


Forming last night, the mob
milled around the Jail here de-
manding that Sheriff Ed Climer
turn over to them the negroes
held in connection with the slay-
ing of Constables Ben Northen
and Millard Brown.


Climer appealed to the governor
for aid and 100 national guards
men were rushed to the jail,
armed with rifles, machine guns
and tear gas bombs. There was
no clash between the two forces.


Held Under Arms


The troops we're withdrawn
from the Jail after the mob dis
persed but we're held under arms
in Nashville ready to return in
the event officers capture George
Oldham, negro, whom Northern
and Brown were attempting to
arrest when they were slain.


The constables followed Old
ham to his home after he was
alleged to have shot and wounded
Sam Smith, white farmer. A
volley of pistol shots from the
cabin killed them instantly. Old
ham escaped, but three negro
men and two negro women in
the house were arrested.


Sheriff Climer removed the five
prisoners to the Nashville Jail.
AS the news of the slayings
spread, crowds of irate white
farmers began pouring into the
town from the surrounding terri
tory.


Lynching Threatened


Several hundred farmers re-
manned in Lebanon after the
attempt on the Jail had been
abandoned. Threats to lynch
Oldham when he is caught caused
officers to maintain the strictest
secrecy about their search for
the negro.

Another program bearing many
distinguished names. and assay
ing notably high in entertain
ment value. is available at Loew'S
Fox Theater this week.


The feature photoplay, "The
Painted Woman" directed by John
Blystone, calls into service the
diversified talents of Spencer
Tracy, Peggy Shannon, William
(Stage) Boyd, Irving Pichel, Paul
Roulien, Murray Kinnell and
Laska Winter.


The story is laid in that always
colorful region known broadly
and generally as "the South
Seas" and, of course, concerns
painted lady who finds love
among the husky he-men there.
Peggy Shannon is the troubled
gal, Bill Boyd is the burly brute,
and Spencer Tracy is the horny
handed but happy-hearted hus-
band.


The reviewer enjoyed "The
Painted Woman" for the forth
right performance of Boyd, the
easy charm of Tracy, and the
natural perfection of Pichels
Characterization. Miss Shannon
struggled desperately with banal
role and did quite as well as any
Hollywood young lady would have
done. 1t is hard to forgive Mr..
Blystone for giving her the newt
able Sadie Thompson photograph.


Many of the scenes are beauti-
full, and newer directorial and pic
torial methods lend this picture a
realism which would have been
utterly lacking a few short years
ago.


The screen program is rounded
out by Movietone News and other
short subjects.


To the stage bill, Pola Negri
brings, in song and dramatic inter
Jude, some of that fire and intense
VividneSs which have marked her
screen appearances.


Pola's reception was cordial,
as was that accorded to that
most gallant trouper, Georges
Carpenter. Carpenter dances a
bit, sings a little, radiates a fine
smile, and let's the girls in his
act help out all along.


Miss Patricola, Wilfred Du
Bots and Joe Phillips add melody
and comedy to the rich stage
fare, and Phil Lampkin with the
orchestra provides the icing.

gust 7. She had been on sick leave
since May.


Miss Mcnamara, a native of Tipton,
was an experienced newspaper woman
who had developed an original style, a
Ightness of touch and a spontaneous
treatment which distinguished her
from less finished writer's.

Miss Mcnamara had been with the
feature service of the local bureau

Miss Mcnamara had worked for the
Des Moines Register, the Omaha Daily
News, the Consolidated Press on the
West Coast and in New York for two
years as g publicity agent.


Covered Coolidge Trip.


She was the only woman reporter to
cover the Black Hills vacation of former
President and Mrs Coolidge. After the
nomination of President Hoover, she
went to his native town of West Branch,
Iowa, to write a series of stories about
the Presidents boyhood West Branch
was near Miss McNamara's own native
town Of Upton and this circumstance
enabled her to pick up local color. which
might have been overlooked by an out
slider.


Miss Mcnamara was member OF
the WomenS Press Club here and well
known in Washington newspaper circles.
She had been working against the hand
leap of i'll health, her friends said, for
some time.


Funeral arrangements have not been
completed. according to word from
Upton. The body is to be cremated.

polluted areas to other bottoms.

oysters will be transferred from these
areas to legal bottoms where they will
lose their impurities within 60 DAYS.

Cambridge will be planted on the
public natural oyster bars nearby, the
commissioner said.

winter and was told that the
New York club, far from wishing

playing days are over, would do
anything within reason to help
him.

that time. But a fortnight ago

BY the Associated Press.


American business men have experi-
enced Chinese boycotts and appreciate
the problem Japan is trying to solve In
its military movement about Shanghai.


The worst boycott against American
interests in China grew out of laws and
regulations excluding Chinese from the
United States. 1t began in 1908 and
was not ended until 1906, involving all
important commercial ports and even
remote interior cities.


In spite of the fact that the Chinese
seem to lack the power Of political or.
ganization, they have unusual ability
to get together in boycotts. Through
commercial and labor guilds they wags
commercial war with a ferocity almost
unbelievable.


Oficials generally disavow any con-
nection. but the movements are 50 well
co-ordinated there is always reason to
believe they are cooperating.


Effects Widely Felt.


Banks, shipping lines, export firms.
retail concerns. schools, missions and
churches all feel the pressure of Chinese
anger. Chinese passengers dare not
sail on steamers of the country against
which the movement is directed.
Chinese firms dare not ship freight


Runs are started on the banks Of the
country, which has given offense.
Servants refuse to work for its nationals.
Retail merchants are forced to conceal
wares originating in the country under
fire. Delegations patrol docks, search
trains and destroy suspected freight.


reign Of terror is inaugurated and
Chinese dare not risk violation of the
boycott orders. Spies are everywhere.
Chinese newspapers carry on agitation.
Posters cover walls and professional
readers in tea houses and on street cor
ners keep the illiterate informed
Even rickshaw men are not permitted
to serve citizens Of the nation which
is being attacked.


Japan has suffered seven or eight
really widespread boycotts in China
since 1908. The 1915 boycott. declared
because of Japans 81 demands in con-
nection with japanese succession to
German rights in Shantung Province,
was very serious. For months japanese
YangtZe River and coastwise ships car
ried no coolies in steerage and were
without freight. Again in 1919 and in
1927 and 1923 disputes about the
Shantung situation inspired boycotts.
The Manchurian clash last September,
when Japan seized Mukden. inspired the
widespread boycott which Japan is
now trying to suppress with arms in
Shanghai.

BY the Associated Press.


TERRE HAUTE Ind, August A.
The siege of the Dixie Bee Coal mine
was raised by the armed forces of the
State today and IS besieged miners
were freed


A union picket line, whose Sniping
held the 65 non-union men prisoners
for two days, faded into the night as
$40 National Guardsmen, heavily
armed, marched to the mine.


Four wounded miners, without medi-
cal attention since Tuesday afternoon,
when they fought rifle battle in which
one picket was killed and four injured,
were brought to Terre Haute hospital.


Haggard from their vigil against pos
sible attacks by the rif1emen encamped
about the mine shaft, the non-unlon
workmen said they believed arrival of
six National Guard planes late yester-
day saved their lives Pickets appeared
to be preparing to rush the mine, they
said, when the first plane swOoped over
the battle line.


Dy


The planes were the advance guard
of the infantry companies ordered here
by Gov. Harry G. Leslie after repeated
urgent requests from Sheriff Joe Dreher,
whose force of deputies was helpless to
combat the well manned picket lime.


An order to bomb the picket positions
with tear gas was countermanded soon
after it was issued last night, but the
pilots maintained a constant patrol over
the area. This surveillance, the be-
sieged miners, believed, cOwed the p1ckets
and ended the bloodiest fight in recent
Indiana mine labor disputes.


Not a picket was to be found when
the guardsmen arrived at the mine this
morning They searched surrounding
thickets for any lurking sniperS, then
took positions protecting the mine
property.


The wounded. who were brought to
Terre Haute, were Gerald Cradle, 26,
Sullivan, shot twice in the right leg
and twice in the right hand: John
Pullman, 81, Terre Haute, bullet wound
in right side; Elmer Bedwell, 26, Sulli-
van, shot in the left arm, and Glenn
Brossman, 81, Terre Haute, who was
struck in the right leg.


Military Rule Declared.





Acting on behalf of Gov. Leslie. Adjt
Gen. Paul E Tombaugh proclaimed the
Dixie Bee Mine and adjacent territory
under military control, effective at $50
last night.


Late last night the Governor, at In
Clanapolis announced the negotiation
of virtual truce of hostilitieS at the
embattled mine. He said after opera
tors of the mine agreed to discontinue
union labor pending a general wage
settlement in the Indiana field, union
representatives telephoned orders to
disband the pickets-


Immediate denial came from officials
who said no officer of the mine had
conferred with the Governor John
Hoke Beasley. attorney for the mine,
issued a statement saying the pickets
had failed to withdraw after tenta-
tive agreement entered into by Ralph
Butler, mine superintendent, under
which the mine would suspend opera
tions for an indefinite period.


Mine officials said today they plan
ned to resume hoisting of coal as soon
as their employees recovered from eff
fects of the long siege.


The appearance of National Guards
men was their second sortie into the
Indiana mine field in two weeks, Gov
Leslie sent four companies to Dugger,
Ind, recently to lift a siege at the CO.
operatively operated Hoosier coal mine.

CHICAGO, June 20 (N,AN.A).-One
slender feminine hand has been discoy-
cred among those of the powerful lead
ers who shift controls in the machine
making politics of the Democratic con-
vention.


The hand belongs to Florence Farley,
national committeewoman from Kan
sas and one of the vice chairmen OF the
National Committee.


Having met her, one never could for
get the shine in her dark eyes as she
talks or the dimple in her chin, that
ADDS piquancy to her smile. But her
touch on the controlling wheels is so
quiet and modest that even keen OBJ
server hardly would suspect the part
she plays.


Mrs. Nellie Tayloe Ross, first vice

gracefully takes the official bows for

magnetic Ruth Bryan Owen, recently

ccmmitteewoman to hear them talk
Meanwhile, the real feminine power OF
The convention sits obscurely in the
background.


Gallery spectators at the stadium
crane their necks to see where Alice
Roosevelt Longworth, who seems to en-
joy a Democratic convention as much
as Republican one. is sitting above the
speakers platform. They identify Mrs.
Woodrow Wilson and they look for Mrs.
Alfred e. Smiths bright features.

Farley of Kansas, whom practically all
the Democratic political bigwigs consult

tional committeewoman longer than any
other Democrat. She was first appoint
ed in 1920 and has served continuously,
winning with 4-to-1 vote this year,
although the Governor of her State

important committees, Managing the
Arrangements, Seating and Tickets
plums usually reserved for important
men.


Most women prominent in politics in

Farley got her training from her pioneer
mother Its efficacy is demonstrated
by the fact that such men as William
Gibbs McAdoo, Jouett Shouse, John j.
Raskob, Glen Shaver, Jesse Jones,
Frank Hague and Joseph Wolf, repre-
senting practically all the various Dem
ocratic camps, are seeking her counsel.


Because of her reticence, Mrs. Far
ley escaped the limelight. When the
Women's National Democratic Clubs
have their breakfast meeting at the
Chicago Women'S Club, Mrs. Farley will
not be featured. Mrs. George Bass of
this city, first woman to serve as vice
chairman of the Democratic National
Committee, will preside. Mrs. ]. Bor-

pheasants. Some States give the eggs free to
qualified persons who will hatch them, raise
the young and liberate them. So here you can
have some splendid pets during the Summer
and release them in the fields before school
starts next Fall Write your game commits
sioner about it,


To hatch pheasants' eggs you will need q
broody bantam very light weight, standard
size hen. Probably you can borrow one from
nearby farm. The nest box ought to be about
one foot square and high, with peat moss or
shavings on the bottom. Be sure that the hen
can have plenty of fresh air, but have no holes
over half an inch either way or the little birds
will escape.


Prepare the nest and test the hen for broodi-
ness for two days. Slide the olive-shaped eggs
under her carefully. Moisten with warm water
three times a week and care for the hen twice
day. Turn the pheasant eggs with your hand
twice day and cool them while the hen Is
eating her cracked corn, exercising and having
drink She should be busted with lice-powder
once a week during the first two weeks.


1t takes ringneck eggs about % days to hatch.
Just as soon as you find the eggs are pipped
the shell crackedD you should return the hen
to the nest carefully and close the cover. Leave
her strictly alone for 4 hours. Then If the
weather is fine the brood is taken to a coop with
the bantam for the first feed This is the same
baby chick starter that is fed to young wild
ducks, as well as to ordinary chicken. Mix it
crumbly-wet with water or milk and give the
pheasants just what they will eat up in few
minutes Take away all uneaten food and mix
the mash fresh for each meal Open the front
door of the coop when the birds are 10 days
to two weeks old. If you wish the bantam can
go out with them. At any rate the pheasants
are ready to be liberated in the fields when
they are three months old

Prof Cannon, in you do not know Is

During the World War he given the Dis

England made him Companion Of the Bath,

finally unveiled portrait OF him. Prof. Can
non, they agreed, has contributed more to
physiology than any living person.


Physiology, If you little vague about 1t,
comes from two Greek words-physio, mean
ing nature, and ology, meaning science. Physi-
ology then, is the science of nature"
Biology is more familiar term and means
about the same thing. Bios was the old Greek
word for life. Biology means the science or
study of life. Prof Cannon studies life IN
living creatures, cats and dogs and men. In
his laboratory he works almost entirely with
cats and dogs but all his findings apply to
men.


You know, of course, that dogs and cats are
natural enemies. Put a strange cat and
barking dog in the same room and see what
happens. Watch the cat first. She Kisses.
She SnarlS And she SpitS. The pupils of her
eyes dilate, and her retract. She bares
her teeth and strikes out with her front paws.
The hairs ON her back and tail stand erect.


The enraged dog capers about. His eyes
flash. He trembles violently. His short hairs
stand literally end.


h low Prof Cannon makes use of this natural
enmity between cats and dogs to pursue
his physiological experiments After five min
utes of intense excitement he subjects both
animals to a medical examination.


Their hearts beating % times per min
ute faster than usual. Their nervous systems
are completely upset and their digeStionS tenn
porarily wrecked. Prof. Cannon X-rays their
stomachs and intestnes and can see exactly
what takes place.


You may have heard of peristaltc activity.
It means the churnng waves in the stomach.
Properly to digest food, these waves, or knead-
ing movements, are necessary.


When Prof Cannon X-rays the laboratory
animals he finds that after five minutes of
violent excitement their digestion is impaired
for IS minutes. PeriStaltic activity ceases. The
little churning Stled. The reason
for this is an involuntary release of adrenalin
from the adrenal glands


This adrenalin is discharged into the blood
stream and raises quite rumpus with virtually
everything in the body. 1t causes rush OF
blood to the heart, the lungs and the brain.
1t makes the heart beat faster and liberates
sugar from the liver into the blood-stream.

NEW YORK, June 25.-While price
changes in the week end stock market
were in general narrow, the movement
itself betrayed nervousness on the part
Of operators for both accounts.


Early selling brought new lows in a
numoer OF pivotal stocks, mostly those
which had been under pressure Friday
but with no increase in volume and
with, in most cases, subsequent re-
covery.


The decline of Friday brought selling
orders into the list at the opening to-
day and new lows were recorded by
American Can, Allied Chemical, United
States Steel, Atchison and American
Telephone. In all of these the losses
we're only fractional. Thereafter rally
and reaction alternated, neither going
very far.


Besides dividend doubts, the market
had the Chicago banking situation to
sppraise Another bank was closed to-
day. the news coming out while trading
was in progress, but the announcement
had no perceptible affect on prices
With the averages flirting with the lows
of the bear movement. the real feature
was the resistance offered, and not the
pressure.


Auburn Auto broke rather sharply,
but that stock is law unto itself.
Under Al today it was down more than
II points from the high of yesterday
and rapidly approaching the level from
which it started its spectacular advance
at the expense of the short interest
early in the month. Among the stocks
which made better than the average
showing was Consolidated Gas, the
earnings statement of which was pub
lished today. For the quarter ending
March 81, 1882. net income was $22,-
493.506, against $25.250,8l5 in the
similar period Of 1881. South Porto
Rico Sugar was in demand again at
approximately the high of the move
ment, anticipating dividend resumption.
Food stocks held their position well and
low-priced oils were steady.


Preferred stocks were irregular. Gen
eral Motors preferred broke through so
for the first time and United States
Steel preferred sold scant fraction
above its old low On the other hand
Firestone Tire & Rubber preferred was
slightly higher The Firestone earn
ings statement for the six months end
ed April 30 showed preferred dividends
covered with cents a share for the
common.


Railroad stocks were unfavorably af-
fected by the weakness in Atchison
which sold today at the lowest since
1900. Great Northern preferred, d.
rectors of which yesterday took no ac-
tion on the dividend, was fractionally
lower but more in sympathy with the
general market than because of the
dividend omission, which had been ex-
pected

ner


When the trade revival arrives, and

The aid extended through Federal

christsned by the Matson Line. third
sister ship, the Lurline, will be turned
out soon to engage in Panama Canal,
Hawaii, or South Seas service.


Other New Liners.


Supplementing three $7,000,000 ships,
the California, Virginia and Pennsyl-
Vania. placed in the intercoaStal Serv-
ice in 1928 and 1929, four $4,000 900
passenger and freight liners have been
projected by the Grace Lines.


The first of these, the Santa Rosa,
was christened a few days ago and
three others. the Santa Elena. Santa
Lucia and Santa Paula, will be COM
misSioned soon. These will engage in
passenger and freight trade between
California and New York by way of
Mexico, Central America, the Canal,
Colombia and Havana.


The South and Central American
West Coast service has felt an equal
stirring for greater luXuriousneSs and,
In the case of the United Fruit Co.
Line, orders resulted for three new
$3,500,000 ships to steam between the
Americas on Pacific trade lanes.


The Talmanaca entered service last
January and two sister ships, the Chiri-
qui and the Antigua, each of 10000

boats in trade now number approx
mately 200, declares that unquestion-
ably business conditions throughout the
world are improving The subsistence

reservations and freight pickup is an
ticipated.

upper hand of the coffee surplus prob
lem by the destruction of accumulated
surpluses and other determined action,
coffee importers believe an improve
ment in trade there can be expected
before the end Of the year.


A slight but general increased de-
mand for bananas has been reflected in
a small but encouraging increase of
freight traffic, and a heavy export of
citrus fruits has featured the season
Prices received have been low, but the

NEW YORK, October 26.-The pro-
fessionals who dominate trading IN the
present market sold stocks this morning
and bought them back this afternoon,
and the net results were negligible.


The market was heavy and reaction
ary all through the first half of the
day, hardened in the afternoon and ad-
vanced in the last hour.


The only significance that could fairly
be attached to the days operations was
that favorable action on the United
States Steel preferred dividend had
cleared up only one of the uncertainties
in the general situation. There were
still formidable obstacles to any sus-
tanned advance in securities.


One Of the chief obstacles was the
continued weakness in commodities.
Wheat sold at new low today, and
that had an unfavorable effect on
stocks.


Silver was down again, sugar was
slightly lower and rubber declined.
Cotton was steady, higher most Of
the time. Sterling rallied after the
sharp break of the two preceding days.


The rush to cover was quite urgent
at the end and the best prices were
made in the last Is minutes. Gold
mining stocks were strong all day, with
Homestake at new years high.


Prices were slightly higher at the
start, but did not hold the gains. Be-
fore the first two hours were over
stocks were selling well under yester-
days close. and that includes United
States Steel common. Satisfaction over
the maintenance of the steel preferred
dividend was tempered by the huge
operating loss shown in the third quar-
ter earnings statement, the largest in
the history of the corporation. It was
argued that the directors would not
have acted favorably on the preferred
dividend If they had not believed that
the business outlook was brighter. but
the market did not reflect that view,


On the other hand the action of
commodity prices was distressing. De-
cember wheat during the morning sold
at the lowest price on record Then
there was anxiety about the railway
situation. meaning the piling up of
fixed charges through loans from the
Reconstruction Finance Corporation.
AS temporary expedient receiverships
may be averted, but there remains the
question of the length of time it will
take increasing earnings to catch up
with the new burden of debt. On top
OF all this was the political campaign.


During the morning American Tele-
phone came down within small frac-
tion Of par, Atchison broke through
the 40 level, Allied Chemical sold off 2
to 3 points, American Can changed
nandS under 48 and other stocks suf-
fered proportionate losses Special
pressure was exerted against Drug, Inc,
National Biscuit and Corn Products.
A good deal of this looked like short
selling. but it brought reluctant sup
port. The market was not active, al
though the turnover was slightly larg-
er than yesterday Professionals still
dominated operations and are likely to
continue to do so until after Novem-
Der 8.

NE w YORK, April 30.-Patriots
turned the clock back 143 years today,
welcomed George Washington to New
York, paraded him on Lower Manhat-
tan, listened to him say farewell to
his Army, followed him up Fifth ave-
nue. and inaugurated him first Presi-
dent of the United States


The all-day pageant marked this
city's formal observance Of the Bicen-
tennial year.


The Father Of His Country set out
from the Jersey shore in a barge when
13 guns doomed at Fort Jay at 10 am.
Two barges carried the costumed party,
with Kenneth Murchison, architect,
impersonating Washington, slowly down
the bay to the end of Manhattan.


Revenue cutters. bright with flags,
led the way, and other steam craft,
unknown in 1889, fanked the barges,
while airplanes oszcled aloft and steam
whistles shrilled. Concealed motors on
the barges chugged, but the sailors,
wearing cooked hats, pulled oars Justify.


Hundreds of school children lined
the waterfront. An imposing row of
silk toppers decorated the stand, worn
by Mayor James j. Walker, Grover
Whalen, DR.. Thomas Darlington, the
grand sachem of Tammany; Gene
Tunney and civic and military notables.


Stepping into the identical coach,
which carried the real Washington to
his inauguration, his impersonator led
the procession through the financial
district, with ticker tape streaming
down from skyscraper windows.

They will all see the same street.
They will all feel the same cold,
the same wearinesS, the same
beWilderment, anger, fear and
Encouragement. They will meet
the same indifference or down.
right brutality.


But, by the end of the day,
some of those men will have
found work and friends. Some
won't. Some will be full Of
hope. Some won't. Why?
Weren't they facing the same
world with the same equip
ment?


No, they weren't.


Actually each man was facing
a different world-THE WORLD
WITHIN HIM. And those secret,
inner worlds were as far apart
as the stars.


One man through the years
had built a world of cherished
resentments, of bitter memories.
of hate, rebellion and spite
the world of a mad dog.


A World of Fear


Another man, with much the
same lot, had built a world
of fear and shame and stealth
the world of a hunted rat.


And still another, battling
with the same outward condi-
tions, had built a world of hope
and courage and fighting conf
dence within himself.


Physically, those men inhabi-
ted the same house, the same
city. Spiritually, they moved
through different worlds; and
as they moved each man gath
cred to himself the things that
suited HIS world.


The man who feared found
that which he feared.


The man who hated found
cause for his hate.


The man who hoped found
an answer to his hope.


You can't control the world
outside you, but you can con-
troll your attitude to that
world; and by controlling that
attitude, you can shape your
life according to your pattern.


That does not mean that you
can have everything you wish
that your prayers will be
answered literally. Unpleasant,
heart breaking things may
happen to you, in spite of your
courage and confidence. You
may lose your job, your health,
your home. Your friends may
betray you. Your dear ones
may die.


YET YOU MAY SURVIVE
ALL THESE THINGS, AND
FEEL PEACE WITHIN YOU,
AND STRENGTH, AND FAITH,
AND EVEN JOY-IF YOUR
INNER WORLD IS HEALTHY
AND HOPEFUL.


Hold on to that thought
during these difficult days.
Grip it with all your spirit,
and pass it on. 1t is the one
thing upon which you can
build. Everything else may
fail you, but YOUR WORLD
will not fail you if you have
built it truly, bravely.

naces. engines and pumps, women's

degrees.

veys also indicate that while visible in
ventories of raw materials in pro-

suming establishments are gagged down

events and particularly through the an

vious week. Building materials were
lower. The third group that declined
vas paint materials. caused by weakness

creased during the past week were fine

Every train from the south bore its

A few could tell their stories, others

unconscious, dying


1t was hard to determine Just what

they lay in the various emergency hos
pitfalls in Camaguey.


The storm first struck, they said dur
ing Tuesday night, and some 500 resi-
dents began moving out of their homes
to the surrounding countryside.


But the rest of the 1000 residents
remained with their belongings. They
lived through l00-mile- hour wind
but little did they dream that behind
it was a 2O-foot wall of water.


Suddenly out of the blackness just
before dawn the crash of fishing
beats in the harbor-70 of them were
destroyed-notified the town it was
doomed.


There was time for little besides mad
dashing for safety that could not be
found anywhere. Jose Diaz, the Santa
Cruz station agent, said hundreds
crowded about five empty box cars on
railway siding. He couldn't say WHY.
unless they thought the cars were too
heavy for the tide % move


Cars Occupants Drowned.

low Chamber inside the cars Then the
main force of the water hit the big
hulks broadside, topping four and

survivor told how his wife was car

powers-the United States, Great
Britain. France, Russia and Japan
were breaking trail today toward new
alignments intended to promote peace
and security.


AS reflected in Associated Press dis
patches from several capitals, their
activity also introduced three powerful
factors into the international problem.
These factors were:


l. Improved relations between Russia
and Japan despite the troublous Man.
churia that lies between them.


2. The proximity Of treaty of non
aggression between France and Russia
stipulating that France will give no aid
to country attacking Russia. and vice
versa.


3. Apparent Anglo American unity at
Geneva, implying that the worlds two
largest naval powers have reached an
agreement in principle to harmonic
their views on disarmament.


Acts as Go-between.


Moscow reports told of better relations
between Japan and Russia, especially
affecting their mutual trouble spot.
Manchuria. The Russian government
has been acting as go-between Chinese
irregular troops and the japanese gov
eminent in disrupted Northern Man.
churia.


The Chinese troops have cut of
large area Of Northern Manchuria from
the world, and several hundred japanese
are held in Manchuli, Just across the
Russian border Half Of these may be
released through the good Offices of the
Soviet. Besides. Russia has been send
ing Japan daily reports on the Man.
churian situation.


Too. Yosuke Matsuoka who will lead
Japan's defense of her Manchurian
policy before the League Of Nations in
November. will first visit Moscow. There
he presumably will seek to ascertain
Russia's attitude toward the Lytton re-
port to the League which condemned
japanese aggression.


Secrecy Covers Possible Pact.


A veil of secrecy, however, covers the
prospect of a non-aggression pact be-
tween these two powers although Russia
has long openly sought such an agree
ment.


Paris dispatches said the new French
disarmament scheme has security sec
ton which is based on the idea OF
STRENGTHENING the Kellogg-Brland pact
outlawing war In line with this
policy" it was learned. authoritatively.
France has virtually reached an agree
ment with Russia on terms OF a non
aggression pact. There was no amplif1-
cation.


Norman Davis. the American repre-
sentative at the Disarmament Confer
enee. went to the French capital today
to talk over disarmament with Premier
Eduoard Herriot.


Mr.. Davis left London last night after
reaching an agreement in principle with
Prime Minister Ramsay Macdonald to
harmonize the Hoover disarmament
proposals and the British viewpoint.


Thresh Out Differences.


It was authoritatively stated that the
conversations between Mr. Davis, Mr..
Macdonald and Sir John Simon. the
foreign secretary. had threshed out the
Anglo American differences to the point
of unity of purpose at Geneva.


1t was not revealed, however. how the
Hoover plan for general one-thlrd
cut in armaments and the British de-
mand for ample naval mobility had
been reconciled.


Mr.. Davis. incidentally, talked with
Tsuneo Matsudaira, the japanese AM
bassador to London and learned what
Japan will propose for naval reduction
to the Disarmament Conference. This
plan has not been publicly revealed, but
is known to be distinct from either the
American or British ideas.


Insinuating itself into all these factors
was President Hoover's latest declaration
that the United States would build her
Navy to parity with the London treaty
if the Disarmament Conference failed.
The conference is now in recess prob
ably until early next year.

Men Do Weaving.


Among the curious customs of the
Jivaros, he found, was that of weaving
and laundering among the men. This
appears to be almost strictly a mascu-
line occupation, in striking contrast to
the rule among almost all other peo-
Piles. The men weave skirts of cotton.
and so careful is the workmanship that
many months sometimes are required
to complete one garment The men
wear nothing else and they wash their
skirts twice daily. Women wear skirts
and blouses. One blouse is the price
of wife.


Stirling describes the Jivaros as well
built, slightly over feet inches tall
and wearing long, black hair The hair
OF the men is permanently waved. Both
men and women paint their faces.
When not spinning or weaving the men
hunt with poison darts, which they
shoot from blowguns, or raid neighbor-
ing tribes. using lances and muzzle-
loading rifles.

creeks of this land that gunpowder will

The moon was right" late last week.

the running weS terrific.


The wolf led the hunt through the
timberlands and down to the swampS
and back to the ridges. The hunters

signaled that the chase was over and

arrived in time to see the dogs, several
slashed and sore, press into the battle

SHANGHAI, Feb. ) (LN.S).
Leaving their ruined dwellings

Chinese residents of Chapel
today continued their head
long flight from Shanghai.


Like rats scurrying from
holes in the wall, thousands
upon thousands of refugees
fled by every avenue of escape
as shells whistled overhead at
the rate of. one a minute.


Passing from the United States
lines into the British section held
by the Royal Scots Fusiliers, l
saw Soochow Creek, the boundary
line between Chapel and the Inter
national Settlement, packed solid
with refugee junks, each carrying
upwards Of SO Chinese, loaded
down with whatever belongings
they could carry.


BOmberS Overhead


A Royal Scots sentry told me
this wild flight was going on day
after day with crowds patiently
waiting at the wharves for a
chance to flee.


Men with packs of bedding on
their shoulders, women carrying
babies, and children with dogs
and chickens under their skinny
arms jam and jostle on the piers.


Now and then some less stout
hearted refugee darts panic
stricken from the crowd into
some sheltering doorway as Jap
anese bombing planes zoom over
head in the direction OF the
Chinese military lines.

Looters behind the japanese
and Chinese lines increased by
the hour. From the settlement
boundaries, men could be seen
entering deserted houses and car
rying off goods and furniture, un-
molested either by Japanese or
Chinese.


Along the boundary road area,
looters were observed lodging
between the japanese and Chi.
nese lines, ignoring the risk OF
death in their desire to pillage
buildings. ,


The French police arrested
three in the French concession,
and on investigation found a
treasure house where "a trunks
filled with valuables looted from
Chapel had been stored.

BY the Associated Press


VIENNA, March 24.-Reliable reports
reaching here today said that serious
student disorders had occurred in
Rumania, and it was definitely known
that King Carol had consented to re-
ceive delegation of university students
to hear their grievances.


AS details of the disorders were re-
ceived here, it was known that uprisings
ocau rcd both at Bucharest and at
Jassy, and that several border points
we're affected.


Political Unrest Seen.


First reports attributed rioting In the
Rumanian capital to restrictive regu-
lations, but later advices indicated
that there was background of political
discomfort involving Communists.


At Bucharest the students tried to
rush the royal palace, but they were
turned away and concentrated their
violence on the Senate Building. Police
and firemcn had their weapons turned
upon themselves, and swo policemen
and Senator were injured before
troops stopped the melee.


The university group at Jassy at
tackled group of officers, two of whom
were severely injured. Members of the
right radical group we're reported to
have stormed a synagogue at JaSsy,
wrecking the interior and then troop
ing through main streets smashing shop
windows.


University Is Closed.


Tbs Jassy gendarmes lowered their
bayonets and fired blanks, and the stu
dents replied with pistol volley from
bsrricaded dormitories. Many were in
jured, although quiet had peen restored
this morning. The university was closed.


After the Bucharest rioters had tried
to storm Carols palace communique
was issued blaming groups of unem-
ployed Communists for mingling with
the student mob. Another report had 1t
that mixed political elements partici-
pated." At any rate Carol took events
seriously enough to announce he would
receive the student delegation shortly.

GLEN ECHO, Nd, February "a
Fire, which for a time threatened the
amusement park here this morning de-

Philosophy, a large abandoned building

years and as it did not have a roof had
become filled with leaves which burned
rapidly and gave off great amount of
smoke. The Glen Echo Fire Company

difficulty from nearby plug, but the

siderable distance. The Chevy Chase
company also responded to the alarm

smoldering several hours after the fire,
and the Glen Echo Department was
standing by to prevent the flames break
ing out anew.

THE ancient science of alchemy never attained
its object, but from the discoveries which
came alcng incidental to the real purposes of
the alchemist founded the great science Of
chemistry.


The ancient alchenlists believed that there
existed solid red substance which was called
philosophers stone or the grand elixer which
was a cure-an for disease and at the same time
had the property of changing base metals into
gold when the philosophers stone and the base
metal were melted together. Another similar
substance. but white IN color, was supposed to
exist which would by the same means produce
silver.
, For many generations the alchemists worked
at their science, which was recognized and
fostered by the rulers of many lands Though
they never produced their philosophers stone
nor their grand elixir, what they did discover in
time came to be worth more than all the gold
they had hoped to produce, and much of medi-
cal science is predicated upon the truths un-
earthed by the alchemists.

HOPEWELL,' N. j., May 13 P1.-
Mount Rose, near which the body OF
Col. Charles A. Lindbergh's son was
found, is hamlet of about half dozen
houses and a general store on the road
connecting Princeton with Hopewell
and about a mile and half from the
latter. During part Of the time that
his Sourland Mountain home was under
construction Col Lindbergh lived in a
house in the hamlet


The village of Hopewell lies between
the Lindbergh home and the scene
where the body was found. The dirt
road leading from the house crosses
the paved highway, which is also the
main street of Hopewell. within the
limits of the town but about eight city
blocks from the center Of habitation.
This road leads into Mount Rose, but
it is virtually untraveled.


Coming from the Lindbergh home,
the kidnapers could have gone into
Mount Rose along that road, turning
there onto the macadam and asphalt
road leading into Princeton, about 7
miles away. The only other manner
in which they could have reached
Mount Rose from the Lindbergh home,
through Stoutsburg and doubling on
their tracks for the greater part of a
mile, was to pass through Hopewell.


The road to Princeton turns of Hope
wells main thoroughfare one block
from the post Office and center of the
town. Along that road, within the city
limits, the kidnapers would have had to
pass several blocks of residences


The fact that the body was found off
the Princeton road and between Mount
Rose and Hopewell indicated that the
child was driven directly through Hope
we'll.


Mount Rose lies near the top Of a
long Sloping hill, from which, in clear
weather, Col Lindbergh's home, about
miles away, is visible. Along parts
of this route, which Is asphalt at that
point, fairly thick and wild woods come
within 10 to IS yards of the road. The
state of wilderness was indicated by the
fact that small animals, such as foxes
and skunks, were seen from time to time
crossing the highway at night at that
point.


The woods in the vicinity, however,
were not combed as the time that Col
Lindbergh and the New Jersey State
police searched through the underbrush,
Immediately after the kidnapping. They
apparently were considered too far from
the home.


1t was along this road that the emer-
gency telephone lines into Col. Lind
bergh's home were strung, partly on
poles and partly on the ground The
road was the principal connection be-
tween Hopewell and the trunk highways
leading from New York, and was used
constantly by police officials and by Col
Lindbergh himself.

charge Of dollar a month or a little

In many sections the rural lines have

operators. who have combined minor
plants at an excessive overhead and
have been unable to meet their dividend
requirements Bond issues have sup
plemented the falling off Of stock sales,

with $4,000 and more stockholders each

BY the Associated Press.


NEW YORK, September 1.-THE
New York Stock Exchange slackened
its grip upon the bears today.


A notice to members said the daily
reports of short positions would be
discontinued and that the short posi-
tion should be reported only as of the
close of business each Monday until
further notice, starting next week.


The exchange also notified members
that they might discontinue the tabula-
ton of the short sales made and COW
cred the same day, known as "out-and-
in" transactions.


Exchange officials made no comment
upon the action, but it was felt in
brokerage circles that since the latest
monthly report had shown bear opera
tions at the smallest volume for any
time since figures became available, 1t
might well have been concluded that
less drastic supervision was called for
The new regulation will eliminate a
vast amount of clerical and statistical
work, both on the part of the exchange
and its members.


The exchange, it was explained, how
ever, will still exercise great care to
prevent bear raids. The regulation that
no short sale may be executed at price
lower than the last sale Of long stock,
was still left IN effect. This, exchange
officials have felt, effectively prevents
selling the market down" by bears.

SAN JOSE, Costa Rica, February 10.
Costa Rica's three-day rebellion led
by a defeated presidential candidate was
ended yesterday by a peace parley.


(The rebels, headed by Manuel Castro
Quesada, the unsuccessful candidate,
were assured of safety, providing they
surrendered and left the country, dis
patches from Panama City indicated)


The peace was arranged in the Amer
lean legation, across the street from the
rebel stronghold, the Bella Vista Bar
racks. The whole civilian population Of
the capital had fed their homes under
the menace of intermittent firing from
the barracks and threat Of the gov
eInment that the rebel position would
be bombarded.


Delegates representing the govern
ment and the discontented faction met
in the legation in the presence of the
entire diplomatic corps to this tiny
Central American republic.


Il am greatly satisfied at the way
Costa Rica has solved its own difficult
ties" said Charles C. Eberhardt, United
States Minister, who had offered his
good offices.


The government later said order had
been restored. Eight dead and 20
wounded-all rebels-were the total
casualties yesterday, the government re-
ported. Four persons, including two
loyalists, previously had been reported
killed and many wounded In street
shooting.


The loyalist army supported Presi-
dent-elect Ricardo JimineZ. The Bella
Vista Barracks were taken over by the
Quesada forces Monday, after the re-
turns from Sundays election went
against them.
