text:
Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, October %. - Stocks
closed the week heavy in another Ses-
sion Of lifeleSs trading. The rally in
progress yesterday was still in evidence
at the opening, but after the car load
ingS statement came out the gains were
Cancelled and prices yielded.


The traffic statement did not come up
to expectations. LoadingS for the week
ending October % were down 8,405 cars
from the previous week. Compared with
the same week year ago they showed
decrease of 16.5 per cent. whereas
the corresponding drop in the figures
given out last Saturday was 14.5 per
cent. 1t could not be said that the rail
stocks were weak. They simply sold
off on small volume, the decline repre-
Senting the evening up of accounts
rather than any real liquidation.


The rest of. the market followed the
lead of the rails more or less. In the
first hour relative strength was dis
played by American Telephone. Allied
Chemical. United States Steel common
and preferred and American Can
These, too Sagged subsequently.


Even stocks which had the benefit
of favorable earning statements were
slow to respond. The Canadian Pacific
in September increased its gross and
net over that month a year ago. but
the stock moved with the rest of the
market, disregarding the better show
ing. South Puerto Rico sugar achieved
a remarkable record in earning over
ESQ a share for its common stock in
the year ending September 30, period
covering the lowest prices in the history
of the sugar industry. The balance
sheet accompanying the income ac-
count revealed great strength, with cash
more than equal to all current liabilities.
However, the stock had discounted this
in the moderate advance of Friday and
only held steady.


One of the steadiest groups was that
including the metal shares. For this
there was no explanation in COM
modify prices, with copper around the
low of the reaction. However, there
was demand for Kennecott on every
setback, some of it said to be for
foreign account. Just why Europe
should be buying our copper stocks
under present conditions is a question
to which the Street had no ready an
swer. Oil stocks were well supported,
but inactive.

God, hold me steady!
Keep me seeing straight
Through all the darkness
OF these treach'rous years.
I learned in childhood
Certain clear cut rules;
Was taught that some few


things


Were always right
Strong, simple things
Like honor, kindliness,
Clean living, courage,
Generosity,
And faith in You.
These things, they told me,
Were worth all they cost,
And would withstand
The shock and shift of Time.
But now-I wonder;
Now I am dismayed;
For all things change,
And have lost Your hand.
The past has vanished
With it's simple code.
The present whirls around me
In a fog.


I tumble blindly,
Fail to find light
And cannot, sometimes,
Tell the Wrong from Right.

And, from the turmoil,
Voices mock and sneer,
And ask what honor buys,
Or decency.
They cry: 80 get 1t
while the getting's good;
you've but one life;
Don't throw this chance away!
And other voices,
Soft and snakey wise.
Uphold new standards;
Say: THE times have changed.
Your fathers code
"Was proper for a child,
But now, you're older.
Turn from fairy tales
"And dare to. face
"The ruthless facts of life"
And so I falter.
Wond'ring where to turn,
While, through the fog,
The tricky half-truths burn
Like will-o'- -wisps
Above a quaking bog.
God, hold me steady!
Help me in my plight!
And in the darkness
Set your laws alight,
Like steadfast stars.
To guide me safely home.

advanced the thought that extremely
low prices now prevailing contain the
seeds for future prosperity. There has
never been prosperity period growing

these economists have stated, and with

bottoms ever reached, the inducement
for business men to start expansion
programs once they are satisfied that

One of the very attractive orna-
mentals now in full bloom is the So
called mimosa tree with its large pin
nate leaves and feathery pink blooms.
Like the Grape myrtle. Just coming into
bloom, this tree reaches its northern
limits in this region and is sometimes
injured during our hardest Winters.
The mimosa is a legume like the locust
and the Kentucky coffee bean, thereby
possessing the capacity for utilizing the
nitrogen supply of the air. 1t is very
rapid grower and is readily produced
from seed. Its low rather spreading
habit of growth does not fit it for the
very small front yard, but it Is really
beautiful on larger suburban places.
The flowers have considerable fragrance.
but have little value for cutting, their
beauty being most striking when on the
tree itself

All this time the sun had been set

oddly Ike the backs Of giant animals

Nick had turned the nose OF the

Spurs Of mountains, dark purple on

bank Of q creek

Judy became aware that there was a
change In the steady churning of the
engine. Now and then it seemed to
cough seemed to miss a stroke,
and when that happened Judy felt fear
freeze like ice about her heart.


She looked around at Nick. This
time there was no reaSsuring smile.
Nick's head was bent over the controls
Now he was pesring sharply over the
edge Of the cockpit searching the
ground below.


The motor was coughing badly now.
A rasping, hollow konk konk. F..

It for danger.


Her heart stood still, then seemed to
turn over, as Nick winged the plane

ernor said negotiations were pending

County since the National Farmers

mcnth ago.

and Sioux City officials were In prospect.

servations of this phenomenon.


1t brings down the icebergs Obserya-

year to year may affect the weather
over much of the Atlantic sector of the
Northern Hemisphere. The ice melts as

warmer water. The cold water from
the melting ice mixes with the Gulf
Stream and cools it. This may result
in cold and storms over Northern
Europe

established, Comdr. Smith said, that
the discharge of the cold currents into
the North Atlantic has approximately

ed from the North Atlantic The great

proportions.

take steps similar to those planned by
the United States. Post office author
tiles said the strike deadlock continued

NEW YORK, July 3o.-Cables and

IONDON.-Basically, British markets

Stock markets have been firm during

it is confidently expected that 1t would

major conversion operation early in the
Fall, each days report from London Of
the success of the British conversion
Is viewed optimistically. Likewise, end
of-the-week reports from Berlin, where
martial law has been withdrawn, Is
viewed more hopefully.


Stock markets firmed during the week
on better reports from Wall Street. on
the hopeful note in Senator BorahS
proposal for debt reduction, and in the
lessening of tension in Germany.


The governments budget committee
is remaining intact in Paris despite the

WINCHESTER, Va, November 19.-
Eula Woofter, 81, of Picketts, w. Va,
was quoted this afternoon by Sheriff
Luther Pannett as having confessed
that she left Jackson, Miss, voluntarily
and came to Virginia with two men
who put her out Of car here.


Earlier the girl had told police and
hospital authorities a story of having
been kidnapped from the Mississippi city
and brought here by the two men, whom
she then said assaulted her and threw
her out of their car.


Questioned by Sheriff.


Sheriff Pannett said that under ques-
tioning the girl admitted that her story
of being the daughter of a railroad
official at Jackson and student at the
University of Mississippi was a hoax.
He said she gave no reason for telling
the tale, but admitted she had been
drinking with the men ON the way to
Virginia and that~When they let her
out of their machine here yesterday
afternoon she started to walk toward
West Virginia. hoping to get ride
home.


She said, according to the sheriff
that the men with whom she had come
North criminally assaulted her on the
road in the vicinity of Gore and then
left her.


Sheriff Pannett said be also had a
telephone message from her father
Robert Woofter, at Picketts, saying his
daughter had left home a year ago and
had not been heard from until reported
here today. He asked that she be de-
tained until relatives could come for
her.


Denies Knowing Men.


Asked by police for the names of the
men with whom she had been travelling
the girl said she did not know them
claiming she merely had been offered
ride from Jackson, where she had
been staying for some time. She said
one was tall and white and the other
a short man, who wore glasses, and
had the appearance of Filipino.


Both were young, she said

Special Dispatch to The Star


HOLLYWOOD, August 25. - They're
going very Russian in Hollywood, and
the latest is a travelogue about the
mysterious lost colony" of Russians
who settled on the Gulf of California
many years ago. The Russians, depart
ing from various spots and people who
proved unfriendly, got lost on purpose.
They knew where they were, even If
the world didn't.


So completely were they successful in
getting lost that they still retain the
old type of customs and costumes with
which they departed for the wilderness.
Their village is barricaded against
strangers, and they look upon cameras
perhaps rightly-as devil boxes"


Nevertheless. Harold Austin made an
expedition with his devil box to the
Russian colony. He found long bearded
men, women and children with fair
hair and remarkably fair compilations
despite the sun tan acquired by success
sive generations in land SO different
from Russia. On behalf of the Metro
Goldwyn- Mayer people. Austin man
aged to persuade some of the older men
and women that the devil box camera
really had no connection with black
magic. Reluctantly they allowed him
to photograph their village in the in
terests of exploration as well as OF the
Russian influence now sweeping the
cinema capital.


On his way back from the lost Rus
sian colony, Austin came upon two ex-
traordinary animal fights. One was
between dog and rattlesnake. The
other, still more unusual, was between
two ENORMOUS desert turtles. The film,
called "Pefils of the Desert" managed,
therefore to contain the only turtle
prize fight ever photographed


incidentally, the film proves that
turtles are more changeable than men.
In spite of the heat, the Russian men
still wear long boards in the desert, but
the turtle, usually a pretty good-tem-
pered creature, develops mean dispo-
sition under the blazing sun. In the
desert the Russia nremains a Russian,
but the turtle thinks it's a rattlesnake
and very nearly proves it.

BY the Associated Press


LA PAZ. Bolivia, December 29.-The
Bolivian war Office announced officially
last night that Paraguayan troops had
been driven from "solidly intrenched
positions" along kilometer 7, scene of
stubborn fighting the last fortnight in
the Gran Chaco.


Heavy losses had been incurred by
the enemy, the war Office statement
said, and fighting is continuing on other
fronts.


Reports Tuesday that Paraguay was
Withdrawing troops from the Gran
Chaco were believed to indicate an
indefinite postponement OF the unde-
clared war between Paraguay and
Bolivia. The rainy season has started
in the Gran Chaco jungle and will seri-
ously hamper troop movements.


In the 50-year boundary dispute be-
tween the two nations Bolivian forces
have this month suffered $4,000 casual
ties either killed or incapacitated and
Paraguay has had $4,000 in the same
status. A dispatch from La Paz Tues
day said that Bolivian troops claimed
a complete victory and Paraguayan
forces were retreating.

UNIONTOWN Pa. March 12-Joslah
v. Thompson, whose assets some two
decades ago totaled $4,000 600, is leav-

and banker collapsed in the court house
Yesterday. Physicians said 1t was a
paralytic stroke but Thompson scofts
at their diagnosis Because he will not
surrender to infirmity, the doctors said
today he can go home in few days:


The mansion awaits, gloomy and cold,

the spacious estate was place OF gayty
and pomp. Now statuary in the grounds
is corroded and broken. Windows are
patched. Within, once gorgeous hang
ings and rich furniture are covered
with dust and shrouded in white covers.

divorced from his wife, lives alone, save

ministers who have asked the United
States Senate to inquire into the situa-

cation soon after arrival in New York.
other members Of the group were the
Rev. Reinhold Niebuhr. The Rev. Came
ron Hall and the Rev. c. Rankin
Barnes.

day. but did not talk to any miners
families. While here they conferred
with representatives of relief organiza-
tions operating in the mine area. They
thanked local officials and citizens for
their hospitality before leaving last
night.

BOSTON, July "a smoldering fire

been overcome by smoke and gas.


Since the arrival of the Hanover in

The gas masks were not sufficient

smoke which poured out from a cargo

When the fire was brought under
control, longshoremen joined flremen in

moss. AS it was being removed, minor
blazes broke out, but were subdued
quickly.

off shore. When the fire was traced to
the No. 8 hold. Capt. Alex Boehme or
dered the matches sealed and live steam
pumped into 1t. This failed to extin-
guish the blaze and the vessel put into
this port for assistantce.


Capt. Boehme said the ship was prac-
tically undamaged by the fire and that
he expected to sail for New York next
week

June "a with a mixed cargo consigned
to New York, Philadelphia and Balti-

Police were prepared today

extortionist who, within the
last 10 days, has made many
threats against Washington

dren.


A trap set and baited to resem-

extortionist absenting himself

Burning Tree Country Club.


Police believed the extortioniSt,

The society matron, who was
threatened with death unless she
left $4,000 near the club at 5 p. m.
yesterday, was expected to hear
from him again.


Telephone Tapped


The woman, whose, name was
not divulged, like several other
Washingtonians. is being guarded
by police and the telephone over
which the threat was received has
been tapped.


Mrs. Richard Porter Davidson,
granddaughter of Mark Hanna,
received another threat yester"
day that her daughter, Daisy,
would be kidnapped.


Fourth Threat Received


The threat, in note, was the
fourth she has received since
Saturday. The note read:


"POlice are pOwerless to help
you. You had better do as I
have told yOu-leave $4,000 at
the grocery store at Florida
Avenue and Twentieth Street."


The note has been turned over
to police and will be compared
by Bureau of Standards officials
with the others received by Wash.
ingtonians.


Voice Held Similar


Police are inclined to the belief
that the threats are being made
by the same person, despite the
fact that each series has been
written on a different typewriter.


The belief has been Strengthened
by the similarly of the voice
which delivered the last telephone
threat at the Davidson home and
at the residence of the unnamed
society matron.


Police have listened in on both
these conversations and noted
a similarity.


Guards still are being main.
tained at the Davidson home and
at the residence of Sir and Lady
Willmott Lewis. whose son, Junior,
was the first threatened.


A number of other persons, in.

Army Air Corps staged a hair
raising aerial show over Wash
ington today in honor of the
visiting Cuban goodwill fliers.


The Cubans arrived at Boiling

their automobile when IL of the
fastest scouting planes Of the Air
Corps took off to start the show.

executed some Of the most daring
individual and formation maneu-

With wings deeply banked they
trimmed the we'll" around the
field like bicycle riders in a velo-
drome. Later they extended their
their aerial maneuving out over
the city. The Cubans watched
the show from the field.

were luncheon guests of the Air

scheduled to lay a wreath on the

text:
The rescue from the sea of Stanislaus
Hausner, the Polish aviator, after he
had been given up for lost in his at
tempted flight from New York to War
saw is paralleled by the discovery in
Australia of two missing German air
men, Bertrand and Clausemann, miss
ing since May II on a hop from
Timor Island to Port Darwin. They
had started from Kiel February % for
a flight around the world by easy
stages When it was reported from
Port Darwin that they were two days
overdue it was believed that they had
gone down in the stormy Timor Sea
Search was at once instituted along
the northern Australian coast and some
tracks and traces of the lost airmen
were found. including the abandoned
airplane with one of the pontoons miss
ing. The men we're found only about
twelve miles from the point where the
plane had been discovered. They had
wandered, however a long distance in
the push. Ihey SubSlSted upon gum
leaves, snails, kangaroo flesh and
lizards for forty-five days. They feared
meeting cannibal blacks. Finally they
met with friendly natives, who sup
piled them with food. Several times
they saw planes lowering over them,
evidently in search of them, but they
were too weak to attract attention
Their plight was more difficult because
of the fact that they suffered from the
comparative rigors of the Australian
Winter prevailing during most of the
time of their wanderings. When they
have recovered from their distressing
conditions they will have story to
tell that will be one Of the thrillers Of
aviation history.

lately into effect the Executive
order, signed by President Hoover
just before he left for the South,
aboliShing the so-called double
roster" of applicants for Federal
jobs.


The order, affecting every
Government position everywhere,
means that beginning today when
an executive asks the Commits
sion to certify three applicants
for vacancy he may not specify
the sex desired, and the Com
mission will certify the top three
on the list whether men or
women.


Miss Jessie Dell, the woman
member of the Commission, con-
siders the measure a victory for
her sex. She worked for it
long time and only recently won
approval for it by Thomas E.
Campbell, president of the Com
mission. These two members, a
majority, then recommended the
so-called "single roster" plan to
the President, who approved it.


George R. Wales, the dissent
ing member of the Commission,
still protests that the measure
will handicap instead of helping
women in the Federal service. He
points out that practically every
roster for the various Federal
jobs now have at the top veterans
and other men entitled to pre-
ference, and that women lower
on the list stand little chance
of getting jobs for a long time
to come

Due to a. disagreement with
the Musicians Union, the Ma
tional Theater Players will close
the 1882 stock season on Satur-
day night, April 80. Next weeks
bill, "On the Spot" will mark the
closing program of the stock
company.


Manager Stephen E. Cochran
said that subscribers will be
given a refund on their 10-week
season reservations.


Two weeks notice was posted
on the theater bulletin board
last Monday night. This followed
official notification from the
Musicians Union that seven men
must be employed for the 1882
stock season.


Last season the stock company
was given a summer concession
of four men as the orchestra
personnel. This year, however,
the Musicians Union demanded
seven men, adding $135 weekly
to operating expense for the cur
rent season. Refusal to accept
these terms was followed by the
announcement that for the two
weeks until closing, the full
winter scale must be paid.


Thus the theater is paying for
seven men until the closing date,
but is not employing them in
the pit.

ELKADER, Iowa, September
5.-Two of Elkader's pigeons,
whose roosting was on q too well
regulated schedule, are hunting a
new perch and the town clock Is
now keeping good time.


The village fathers had been
puzzled as to why the clock would
gain time the first half of each
hour and lose time the second
half.


They found the pigeons would
hop cnto the clocks big hand
when it was about 10 minutes
after the hour. Their weight
speeded up the machinery and
the clock gained time until the
hand pointed downward at such
an angle that they lost their
perch.


The birds would return when
the hand neared the last quarter
hour and ride upward several
minutes, causing the clock to run
slower.

Q.NS)-Two men were killed

injured early today when the
Maple Leaf express of the Grand
Trunk Railroad was wrecked as
it sped through the city.


James Groves, the engineer,
and Walter Schinning, the fire
man, both of Battle Greek, Mich,
were scalded to death.

burn and his young son, Marshall,
who were crushed when one of

embankment. The locomotive

embankment. one of the baggage

home.

baggage coaches off the roadbed.

ST. JOHNS, N. F., April 6
(I.N.S. ).-World War veterans
today were in control of the
city following a riot staged
by 10000 civilians who stormed
the House of Assembly,
wrecked the building, and
forced the resignation of the
government. Scores were
injured.


Police, who we're powerless in last
nights demonstration, we're still
unable to maintain order today.
Citizens obeyed only World War
officers and the veterans under
them on the streets of the capital,
while most of the police were
bottled up in the assembly build
ing by an irate crowd which
milled outside.


Premier Resigns


The war veterans closely
guarded the private residence of
Prime Minister Sir Richard
Squires, who narrowly escaped
serious injury in the riot.


The crowd remained turbulent
until the resignation of the Pre-
mier had been announced, after
which a Semblance of order was
restored.


Soon after the premier's resig-
nation had been made public,
other government officials handed
in their designations to the gov
ernor.


During the riot a government
liquor store on the grounds was
raided and looted.


The outbreak, in which stones
were hurled, windows smashed,
and many persons injured, was
the elimination of months of dis
tress from unemployment and dis
satisfaction with the government
policy.


Two policemen and two civilians
were taken to hospital with seri-
Gus injuries.


Tear Down Fences


The disturbance was not pre-
meditated. 1t began with an
orderly march of the 10000, COM
prising men, women, and chill
dren, to the capital to demand an
official investigation of charges
that the minutes of the executive
council had been falsely written.
The demand had repeatedly been
refused.


The march was orderly, and the
crowd waited for some time out
side the building while its spokes-
man attempted to gain an inter
view with officials. Parliament
was in session.


Finally, irked at the delay, one
portion of the mob began break
ing down fences for weapons with
which to pass the police lines and
enter the building. The riot was
general Immediately.


The prime minister, the police
chief, and several policemen we're
held captive for several hours in
the executive chamber. which was
guarded effectively as the attack
ing civilians threatened to throw
Sir Richard into the harbor.

guage and culture-a formidable task

tee to write four volume History of

AUBURNDALE, Mass. July .
Political agitation industrial Stagnation
and new lows in security values have
not forcefully affected commodity
prices in recent weeks.


During the past week the average
price level of ! commodities registered
the third consecutive increase. While
the magnitude of the movement was
only fractional, yet three weeks up
ward trend, without interruption. in
the face of adverse economic condi-
tions, indicates price stability. Out Of
IA individual groups curing the week
Just closed five averaged fractionally
higher, six groups were moderately
lower. while three remain unchanged


Industrial prices held steady and
have not moved downward since early
June. The stabilizing influence Is
noted first in the unprecedented and
radical price decline which measures
nearly 49 per cent from 1929, and sec
end. the narrowing ratio OF new pro-
duction as compared with actual
consumption.


Agricultural prices were one of the
six groups that declined, although the
drop was extremely small For well
over a month prices Of farm products
have held relatively steady, despite
large reserve stocks and improved
growing conditions for this years crops


Live stock prices continued the ad-
vance which started several weeks ago
The price recovery was largely respon-
sible for the upturn in the average Of
all commodities.


Textiles also recorded considerabl
strength led by cotton. Since the low
point of cents a pound. cotton has
advanced nearly cent. Coarse textiles
were also fractionslly higher. The two
other groups which recorded price
strength during the week were vegetable
oils and hides and leather.


Building materials prices dropped to
new low point due entirely to the
further lowering in the price level of
lumber. Latest data show that de-
spite production curtailment stocks at
the mills are relatively heavy in terms
of current and near-term prospective
consumption.


The three groups which showed no
price change during the week were
industrial commodities, chemicals, paper
and pulp.

DETROIT, October 10.-Secret serv-

and a printing press to which, they
said, had been traced many counterfeit
IS and $40 bills found in circulation
recently in the East and the Middle
West.


Two men were arrested. They gave
their names as Tom Evanoff, SO, and
Tom Ali, both of Detroit. The print
ing press and plates were found, the
officers said, in Evanoff's room in the
lodging house


Bert Brown. chief of the secret service
here, said the arrests climaxed nine
months search which was started with
the arrests of three men in Pittsburgh
for passing bogus currency.


Brown said the plates and the press
were among the best he had ever seen.
The press worked SO silently, he said.
that others in the lodging house could
not hear it working.


Evanoff, Brown said. was the printer,
and Ali the distributor. The officers
said they found 500 bogus bills of 81
denomination under a mattress in
Evanoff's room.


Brown said the men followed the
custom of counterfeiters in not circu-
l9ting the spurious currency in the city
were it was made.

years war in 1865.

hODpd tn crIlsh fhe main rebel army

Professional and society classes in Sac

sist indefinitely


The break between Argentina and

question. All along the Mississippi

BY the Associated Press.


NEW YORK, October 22.-One
prisoner was killed and many injured
today in rioting at the City Peniten-
tiary on Welfare Island which started
in fighting among prison peace
makers" in the wardens Office.


Two committees of peace makers had
met with the warden to settle racial
animosities which had broken out be-
tween Irish and Italian prisoners.


The peace makers suddenly began
fighting and George Holshod was stab
bed to death. The killing was the
signal for general rioting, which spread
among some 200 prisoners of the 1850
confined in the institution.


The rioting continued for half an
hour before it was quelled and many
were injured in the fighting.


The riot caused one of the greatest
concentrations of police in years, be-
tween 600 and 800 policemen, emergency
squads, police boats and airplanes being
sent to the scene


The police army was equipped with
machine guns, rifles, revolvers and tear
gas bombs


The committees. consisting of about
four men each, began their conversa-
tion peaceably, but soon argument
waxed hot and the peacemakers began
punching at each other. This brawl
was quickly stopped and the commit
teemen went out of the wardens Office.
They began fighting again in the cor
ridor, however, and Holshod was stab
bed to death.

HOPEWELL, N. j., March
16 (IN.S.).-"If" is a banned
word in the household of Col.
Charles A. Lindbergh.


While the rest of the world
talks about eff" the kidnapped
child will be returned, the
famous aviator and his wife
say when" young Charlie is
returned.


In the face of overwhelming
encouragement in the hunt for
their missing son, they cling to
the spoken belief that some day,
somehow, the child will be
brought home.


This was confided to Interna-
tional News Service today by an
intimate friend of the family.


Hold Abiding Hope


Asked if the Lindberghs would
continue to dwell in their big
white house on Sourland Noun
tain, the friend said:


"They will stay right where
they are waiting for the baby's
return.


"YOu can't mention the word
If to the Lindberghs. They
will not think of anything but
the baby's safe return. They
could not go on unless they
believed they will see him
again"


But how Iong?"


Always"


The household has settled down
to routine, however. No house
hold could continue under the
terrific strain that was placed on
the Lindbergh family those first
few days after the baby was
lifted from his crib and spirited
away. Eating, sleeping, doing
normal things like walking or
reading were dispensed with en-.
tirely. The whole family, includ'
ing Mrs. Dwight Morrow, mother

and drank coffee at odd moments
and scarcely ever went to bed at
night.


Regularity Prevails


All that is change. Now meals
are served at regular huorS, and
Mrs. Lindbergh and Mrs. Morrow
go to bed early at night.


Colonel Lindbergh still sits up
until past midnight, waiting for
the telephone to ring with the au.
thentic message that his child is
ready for delivery-some place.
But even he has learned that
strong constitutions and iron
nerves, too. require proper nour'
ishment and some sleep.


The practice of having all
food bought in Englewood, where
the Morrow servants are tending
a decreased family-Mrs. Morrow
remains in Hopewell with her
married daughter, while Miss
Elisabeth Morrow runs the Engle.
wood house-has been discon.
tinued. Now food is purchased in
the local stores and prepared by
the Lindbergh servants, Mr.. and
Mrs. Ollie Wheatley, butler and
cook, and Betty Cow. the van.
iShed baby's nurse.


Every morning and afternoon
Mrs. Lindbergh goes for short
stroll with her mother. Some
times the Colonel and the wire
haired fox terrier accompany
them.


Few police are in the house
now, although about half a dozen
still make their headquarters in

MINNEAPOLIS, July l5.-Twenty-
months old Leslie >Delano, sought six
days as a possible kidnapping victim, was
found yesterday, dead.


His body was recovered from cess
pool near his suburban Columbia
Heights home, just a few hours before
the 125 National Guardsmen, who aided
police and neighbors in a widespread
hunt, were to have been recalled.


Possible Staying Probed.


Whether the son Of Mr.. and Mrs.
Ray Delano met an accidental death
or was slain, Coroner c. B. Thurston
was unable to determine. He planned
further inquiry today.


Thurston said he was unable to de-
eide how long the baby had been dead,
but indications were death had oc-
cured from one to three days ago.


The catch basin. part of a sewage
system of considerable length $50 feet
from the Delano home, had been ex-
amined Sunday by Columbia Heights
police


The sewage line connects several
homes of the neighborhood with a
nearby swamp and investigators said
the boy might have fallen into the
system at another point and the body
have been washed into the basin after
recent heavy rains.


Shaft Is Inspected.


The 15-foot wooden shaft of the cess
pool and its 10-inch square covering
were removed for inspection. The shaft
was studded with nails which might
have caused, authorities said, the
abrasions on the child's legs.


Leslie was last seen alive by a neigh
Dor boy half hour after his mother
had missed him.

HONOLULU, May Mrs Thalia

Mrs. Massie had planned to sail to-

Two policemen. Dewey Mookini and

Pearl Harbor after the public prosecu-
tor, John G. Kelley. had been assured
naval authorities would permit its serv-
ice. The Navy Yard is Government
reservation.

city with the assurance of naval authori-
ties that they would be notified as soon
as Mrs. Massie could be found.

first to the gate of the navy yard to
check their guns. Then they drove TO
the administration building and paid
their respects to Rear Admiral Yates
Stirling. From there they travelled to
the old ship Alton.

MasSie and Mrs Fortescue, but not Mrs.
Massie Both said they did not know
the whereabouts of Mrs MaSsle. The
policemen reported officers on the ship
also said they did not know where she
had gone.


Believe She'll Sail.


Admiral Stirling instructed Capt. F, j
Horne. his chief of staff, to conduct a
search.


Since all the Massie party had
planned to sail tomorrow on the liner
Malolo. friends were of the unanimous
opinion that Mrs. MasSie would be
aboard when it clears the harbor.


officials considered Mrs. Massie had
no intention of remaining here for the
retrial of her alleged attackers and had
baked the efforts of the Territory to
keep her from leaving with her husband

From the San Antonio Evening News.


Many Texas farmers are planning to
produce a cotton crop on last years
stalks. Because of abundant Winter
rains and the absence of frost, plants In
numerous fields are growing green and
some are blooming. Ordinarily the old
stalks would have been plowed under
to lessen the boil weevils, but wet
weather has kept most farmers out Of
the fields. Insects probably will be
more numerous than the average, but
the Winter has been so mild that plow-
ing would not have reduced them great
ly. Cultivating the volunteer" cotton
will have one advantage-perhaps the
bolls will mature before the bugs re-
appear in destructive hosts.


Growing early cotton from the old
stalks was a regular industry along the
Texas Gulf Coast until the process was
found to favor the weevilS multiplca-
ton. This method speeds up the
harvest by several weeks, of course. 1t
is recalled that by such means an en-
terprising Duval County farmer took
first-bale premium for several seasons
until the exchanges ruled volunteer cot
ton out of the competition. Though
some planters assert that such farming
will not violate the acreage-reduction
law, it will not release them from a
moral-and economic-obligation to
grow cotton on but 80 per cent of their
land.

NEW YORK, June 18-The love of
a mother for her child is the story of
Mrs. Rose Hammitt.


Like so many who lived on moored
barges, she cannot swim. Yet when
her 3-year-old son, Erich, tumbled
overheard yesterday, she ran quickly to
the side of the barge and leaped over
board.


She could not swim; but air, trapped
in her clothing as she dropped, feet
first, into the water, buoyed her. Her
screams brought rescue boat which
arrived, as she lay in the water, face
under and slowly sinking.


1t appeared as though her heroism
had been in vain; but when they pulled
her, unconscious, into the boat they
found, locked in her arms, her little
boy.


They will live.

One convict was wounded, dining

ened by fire in riot at the Utah State

Jesus Areso. prisoner, was shot In

Top" among the prisoners because Of his

probably referred to the prison rations.

1t was the saddest parade Washington

drab, weary. colorless tragedy. Tint

By the Associated Press.


GENEVA, Switzerland, February 90
In the three weeks since 1t began, the
International Disarmament Conference
has heard 236 900 words of speeches
and has felt the disagreeable reaction
to outside affairs.


The fall Of the French government
deprived that countrys delegation Of
official standing and prevented the con-
ference from taking any executive
action.


The situation Is similar to that which
disturbed the London Naval Confer
ence at the time of the downfall Of
the Tardieu government. The Execu-
tive Committees of the present confer
ence now must mark time until the
French political crisis is settled.


Meantime the general sessions have
continued with speeches by delegates
from the smaller countries. Monday
and Tuesday will be holidays and
Wednesday will bring three more
speeches.


The situation in the Far East has
been another disturbing factor. The
special session Of the League of Ma
tions Assembly, called for March to
discuss that issue, will distract atten-
ton from the disarmament conference,
but If the French crisis is settled BY
that time the work of the conference
can go on.


The high point this week was the
presentation of Germanys proposal
that all nations disarm to the point
forced upon Germany by the Versailles
Treaty.


This met with sharply unfavorable
reaction from France and her allies,
but was supported in some points by
the United States, Great Britain and
Italy.


Now the conference has before It
two extreme plans-the French project
for an international police force and
very little disarmament, and the Ger
man plan rejecting the international
force and providing for very consider
able disarmament. Its task is to find
middle ground.

civil disobedience movement other than

serve year in prison today.

It was a rip snorting, pyro-

through spring, summer and into
the autumn of last year. Then

formation.


Last spring many Of the spots
that were places of revelry and
high jinks a year before had
closed their doors. Others hung
on grimly anticipating that
patronage would return. There
was the wild hope that the Baer-
Levinsky brawl July 4 would
bring a vast army-with money.


But the holiday influx was
small and those who came to
gamble used five-cent chips on
the wheel and two-blt pieces in
the dice game.


Hotels Lack Guests


Hotel keepers and rooming
house proprietors who took full
advantage of the golden oppor.
tunity of a year ago to ask
double.top prices for lodging, now
are angling for guests-without
luck. The exodus continues, and
thousands who sought Reno for
habitation because Of jobs in
hotels, restaurants, gambling
places, ETC., long since have gone.


Divorce seekers are few and be-
coming fewer and those who are
parked there are neither frivolous
nor gay, perhaps because they
are minus funds for purposes
other than to live modeStly and
pay the legal fees.

NEW YORK. April 2O.-True to its
recent form, today's stock market was
mixture of liquidation in industrials
that used TO be called pivotal and Of
stubborn resistance to pressure by the
rails. There was the usual list of new
lows, Including such prominent victims
as United States Steel common and
preferred, American Telephone and
American Can, but all through the
weakness elsewhere. the carrier stocks
were conspicuously firm.


There was nothing especially un-
favorable in the news. Electric output
was off again on the week compared
with year ago, but the rate Of de-
cline was lower than last week.


Among the features of the last hour
were the selling of the Bush Terminal
issues and buying in Woolworth.


The opening was higher and the
overnight orders gave the impression
that some outside buying, long lacking,
was coming into the market. The rails
made the best showing, as they did yes
terday. For this the reason assigned
was the car loading statement, which,
although down slightly on the week,
and Of course very much under the re-
turns Of year ago. did reveal an in
crease of miscellaneous merchandise
and less-than-carload freight. The fall
ing off was largely in coal traffic.


Atchison was the leader, with Chesa-
peake & Ohio close second so far as
activity was concerned. The former ran
up 2 TO points. Union Pacific on a
smaller turnover was up over 3 points.


This mild demonstration in the rails
temporarily helped the rest of the list.
But Allied Chemical and American Can
were again in supply and both made
new lows for the bear market. So did
Air Reduction. General Electric sold
under Si4 share for the first time, but
made better resistance than yesterday.
During the morning United States Steel
was never very far away from the 80
mark, but the preferred stock went to
a new low.

A LII living things-both plant and animal
I lived at first, millions and millions of
years ago, in the ocean. Gradually when by
chance one or another plant got its head
above the salt water and found the sunshine
quite pleasant, the plants dared to grow taller,
until millions of years later they came to be
uees-not like those we know now, but ferns
and moses, hundred feet tall and wide as
both your arms, growing thickly together in
the marsh All of this took millions of years
millions.


Then something else happened


The trunks of the oldest fern trees became
weak and were crowded until they fell over to
make room for the younger and stronger. They
fell into the water, but they did not rot in
these salty marshes. Gradually more fell until
there was layer of huge trunks Of dead trees.
After layer more than a hundred feet thick
lay there the sand was washed in by the sea,
and mud was carried to them by the rivers,
and this great layer of dead trees was slowly
buried deep below the surface of the earth.
Hundreds and thousands and millions of years
passed, and deeper and deeper the ancient
trees were buried by the sand and mud.


All the while deepening layers Of mud and
sand grew heavier and heavier on the trees
below, pushing harder and harder The sand
and mud above were pressed into layers of
stone, shale, sandstone and slate. Slowly the
heat and the heavy pressure changed the trees
into carbon or coal. Then one year there
was q great crumbling of the earth's crust
and the layers of stone and the carbon which
had once been trees were lifted high above
the level of the sea.


And now ages after the time when the trees
first thrust themselves from the swamp, men
living all over the face of the earth dig about
In its crust to mine the coal under the rocks.


This very winter, scarcely giving 1t thought,
We burn in our furnaces what's left OF giant
forest changed by millions of years.

NASSAU, Bahamas, September 10
A relief expedition was on It's way to-
day to Abaco Island of the Bahamas
group where, 1t was learned yesterday,
IL persons were killed and many in
jured in storm and tidal wave last
Monday.


Quackenbush and including several
Abaro members of the Bahaman Legis-
lature, started last night for the island


The discovery of the disastrous effect
of the storm was made yesterday by
government officials, who visited the
island in an airplane. There was great
need for food, water and supplies, they
said.


Many Buildings Wrecked.


Six settlements were struck and most
of the buildings wrecked. In one settle
ment the only remaining shelter was a
house the roof Of which was blown off


No news had been received from the
island all week.


The largest death list was at Green
Turtle Cay. where six persons were
killed. Twenty-Five were injured. All
houses, churches. schools and govern
ment buildings were reported destroyed.


Inhabitants at Green Turtle Cay said
four persons whose names were not
known were reported dead at Coopers
Town, and that only six houses are
left there.


At Great Guiana Cay one man was
killed. All boats were destroyed and
only four houses, partly damaged, were
left standing.


Burial Ground Washed Away.


Bluff Point was virtually destroyed,
and the burial ground was washed away
in the tidal wave which swept over the
cay. Five persons were injured.


At Marsh Harbor. the first settlement
to feel the height of the storm. schools,
the teachers residence and IL other
houses were destroyed. Most of the
remainder Of the homes were damaged
badly. No one was killed or injured.
but crops and fruit orchards were de-
streyed and two government wharves
we're demolished


At Hupetown SO houses were de-
stroyed and 63 damaged badly, while
40 more received lesser damages. All
public buildings and the radio station

dead reported and only two injured.

The wholesale price index of the
Federal Government today reached its
lowest point since the depression began.


The Labor Departments Bureau Of
Statistics said the index number de-
rived from price quotations Of 784 COM
modities, weighted according to their
Importance, dropped six-tenths of / per
cent during the week, which brought
the level below that of the week Of
June 18, when previous low point was
reached.


The bureau said the commodity
groups which have pulled the price level
to a new low are hides and leather
products, textile products, metals and
metal products. chemical and drugs and
miscellaneous articles.


All these groups, the records show
are below the figures Of June 18 Farm
prices and foods are still slightly above
the June low. alcng with fuel and light
Ing and building materials.


Only three of the 10 major commodity
groups failed to develop weakness last
week, and they remained at the same
level Of the preceding week, according
to the bureau These groups were mis-
cellaneous products. housefurnishing
goods and metals and metal products.
They, however, have slumped decidedly
during the last so days.


Farm products, once IL per cent
above the level Of June 18, are now only
8 per cent higher. while foods, which
had climbed 6.8 per cent, are now only
2 per cent above the June low.

stretches spots which gladden. those who

cylindrical, blunt at both ends and
about inch long. The scales are
downy and three-lobed. with broad
wing which helps them ride the wind.
When the tree Is cut down it sends
shoots out at once and soon the un-
slightly stump has vigorous branches
coming from it. The lumbermen have
"corned this tree because of its size:
however, lately there has been such a
demand for the wood that they are CIV
ing it more respectful consideration.
Shoe pegs, spools. wood-pulp and fuel
are the uses to which the wood is put.

Though the French have brought
highways, hotels, written law and many
other modern Improvements to Morocco,
ancient cWtonls dating back thou
sand yearS persist in Tangier, FeZ,
Meknes, Rabat and other cities, ac-
cording to motion pictures last evening
before members of the National Geo
graphic Society at the Washington Au-
ditorium, shown by Capt. Carl Won
Hoffman.


The "land Of the saints and bandits"
Is difficult to photograph because Of the
Mohammedan prejudice against the
camera plus the unwillingness of women
to lift their wells. Yet the traveller, by
visits over series of years, managed
to obtain motion pictures of the indus
tries, market places, tribal types of men
and women and even interiors OF the
elaborate harems. including the wom-
ems apartments, which are even barred
to native men.


Capt Won Hoffman's picture excur-
sions led him into holy streets where
no Europeans are allowed to shrine
where cuckoo clocks are ornaments
against backgrounds of ancient mosaic
and to the graveyards which serve also
as burial places for the women.


Some Of the most remarkable pictures
obtained were those of native tailors,
sitting in rows along the streets, while
boys hold their thread; the mat weav-
ers, the clothesmakers, the basketry
workers and the processes of making
the leather goods for which Morocco is
famous.


Native dancers using the castinets
were shown, and the speaker explained
that these, like bull fights. were native
to Morocco, and we're introduced into
Spain by the Moors.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


LEONARDTOWN, Md, September 2.
The American liner America, towed
by seven naval tugs, came into the
graveyard Of interned ships in the
mouth of the Patuxent River on the
Chesapeake Bay today of Milestone
Landing. II miles below here.


The ship, a former North German
Lloyd liner, was interned, and subse-
quently seized by the Government when
the United States entered the World
War, operated as Navy transport, and
after that was modernized and put
back into the North Atlantic passenger
service by the Shipping Board. She
then gained fame under Capt. Fried,
who made daring rescues at sea. She
Joined her sister ship, the George
Washington, which arrived last Thurs
day, and was moored near here.


The two other ships moored there
and have been for some three years,
are the Mount Vernon, originally the
Kaiser Wilhelm, and the Agamemnon,
originally the Princess Cecilia.

NEW YORK, March 30-After open
ing higher, stocks on the Curb Exchange
turned irregular around midday and
trading slackened.


Taken as a group, petroleum shares
made the most uniformly upward show
ing, while public utilities furnished a
contrast on the downward side. Electric
Bond g. Share was OF about a half
point. Standard Oil of Indiana was
steady, and so was Cities Service, while
Gulf Oil at times was up point.


Most of the midweek reviews were
constructive. The electrical output fig
ures, however, were down 1913 per cent
from the preceding week, which in turn
was of 8.6 per cent, thereby bringing
national electric output for last week
to the lowest level Of the depression
period. The Pacific Coast territory for
the second time registered the widest
decline, with the Chicago industrial
region second The central industrial
and Atlantic seaboard regions recorded
the smallest losses, both indicating
some firming In production activities.


Prospective early settlement of the
coal strike, along with the proposed
tax on coal imports, enabled Glen Al
den to absorb offerings readily and
Lehigh Coal & Navigation to open up
point. Deferring of the quarterly
common and preferred dividends on
Valvoline Oil, which paid the regular

marketwise.

Lois went to market early and found
hot the proverbial worm-bS Bar
gains. Fresh raspberries and currants
that had been picked so recently they
still looked dewy were more than she
could resist. So back home she came
with her days work laid out for her.


She sat herself on the porch where
there was breeze, and just enough
sun to give Ann her sun bath.


Ann played with her doll and her
books, keeping watchful eye on her
mother. She hoped somehow that a
red currant or two would roll down her
way. She thought she never had seen
such pretty little balls.


Lois decided to make some red rasp-
berry and currant jam. She used the
proportion of three-quarters as much
sugar by weight as she had fruit. That
Is. for every pound of fruit she used
three-quarters OF pound Of sugar.


She put layer of fruit in the bot
tom of the preserving kettle. sprinkled
generously with sugar, mashed the fruit
and then added a second layer of fruit
and sugar. BY MASKING these two lay
erS she had enough Juice to start the
cooking with no danger of burning the
jam. The rest of fruit and sugar was
now added and the mixture cooked
until teaspoonful of the mixture,
cooled quickly. was Of thick or jam
like consistency.


She might have washed currants,
cooked them separately and then ex-
tracted juice, measured that. added red
raspberries and required sugar and
cooked the mixture Or she might
have cooked the currant juice and COM
plete amount of sugar almost to a
jelly degree and then put in the ad-
ditional raspberries, cooking them for
10 minutes. This would have given her
a clear jelly with whole raspberries
floating in it.

tors include: The lack of a balanced
budget, the political conventions. the
Lausanne Disarmament Conference

tons. Favorable factors include: Re-
duction in debt-the Bank for Inter-
national Settlements within the last
year has liquidated go per cent of in
ternational short-term Indebtedness
gradual regaining of economic balance;
realization of need for international
cooperation and realization that there
is no legislative cure-all for the present
situation and that no permanent gain
would be made in debasing the cur
rency.

WELLINGTON, New Zealand,
Sept. 16 0.N.S0.-A severe earth
quake shook 60-mile area sur
rounding Hastings, Napier, Gis-
borne and Wairoa today, throw
ing the entire population into
panic.


The tremors continued through
out the day, accompanied by
a downpour of rain which caused
huge landslides. Damage was
great everywhere in the affected
areas. although only three in
juries were reported.


One landslide blocked the high
way between Bisborne and Wal
roa, where 100000 tons of earth
and rock were estimated to have
fallen.


Many of the buildings which
were damaged in the earthquake
of 1881 collapsed under the
strain.


Hundreds of chimneys and
walls fell at Osborne, including
the wall of the Anglican church
there.


The postoffice and other build
ings were badly cracked.


The quake also made huge
cracks in the roads about Mairoa,
where bridges collapsed and the
water supply was interrupted.

CHICAGO, August 25.-Misstng: One
brewery owned by the United States
Government.


Federal officials. puzzled over what
to do with the old Standard Brewery
formerly owned by Terry Druggan and
Frank Lake, found their problem solved
for them yesterday.
They visited the former deliberately
equipped brewery and found little more
than four brick walls and a roof-and
the walls weren't complete, either.


Police said they believed the wood
work and flooring had been cut up and
carried away by the poor residents of
the neighborhood for kindling wood,
that the copper vats and piping and
other metal was stolen to be sold for
junk, and that some Of the bricks were
taken from the walls by the homeless
to build shacks.


The brewery was seized several years
ago on an income tax lien against
Druggan and Lake, who now are serving
prison sentences for income tax evasion.
Efforts to sell the brewery at auction
failed.

Some of the old countryfolk who re-

meal as supper" Those who don't

benches along the wall of the audi

fork in the road, few miles north of
Hyde Park.

from the farms and the village. With
them will ningle the Governor s family
and the friends who have worked with

office.

CHARLES CITY, Iowa, August %
Indignation over varied wages they
said were paid from the city relief
fund. party of unemployed men yes
terday abducted Miss Marion Stull.
Floyd County overSeer of the poor, and
held her prisoner for several hours.


She was released after being struck

Charles City.


Five of the seven men who accom-
panied her on the automobile ride were
among eleven later arrested by authori
ties and charged with conspiracy and
kidnapping,


Can Identify Men.


Miss Stull said she did not know

would be able to identify them.


Dissatisfaction over the maximum
wage of SIPS paid woodcutters from
the unemployment relief was blamed
for the trouble. Unemployed men put

the Woodcutters asserted. adding they
were forced to work nine hours.


Between SO and IS workers invaded

arrival in the morning. When she ap-
peared they forced her into the car
with the seven men and sped away. A
hastily organized automobile posse lost
the trail when the abductors changed
their route and returned to Charles
City, where they took Miss Stulls au-
tomobile.


Released Miles Away.


Then they continued to New Hamp-
ton, where they released her and aban-
doned her car. She drove to Alta Vista,
10 miles north of New Hampton and
telephoned Mayor G. c. Gray here
that she was safe.


Miss Stull said the men had beaten
her, twisted her knees and struck her
in the back of the head until she lost
consciousness. Bruises were found on
her arms and head, but she was not
seriously hurt.


She identified Chester Coving, one
of those under arrest, as one of the
men who struck her. Others arrested
whom she identified as members Of the
abducting party were Don Dodd, John
Bauer, Joe Sievers and Ellwood Moh-
ring

said to be the president of the county
Unemployed Association: Kenneth En-
erson, James Smith, Girvin Hutton.

man, Wayne Chapman.

Miss Stull said all of the arrested

relief works. They had first worked on
the road and garden projects, but when
that work ran out they were shifted
to the wood cutting at the reduced pay.


She said that, while the maximum
cash wage per day for woodcutters was
SIPS. food supplies could be earned
by cutting more than one cord. She
added that the number Of days Of work
provided per week depended uDon the

The workers denied that they had an
opportunity to earn groceries in addi-
ton to their pay and claimed that Miss
Stull had not treated them with proper
respect The county Board of Su-

Bruening government placed on the Ma

text will not be published until tomor-

until Friday.

demonstrations still stands.


Likewise the Bavarian government
pointed out that long before the storm
troops were dissolved it had issued a
general ban on uniforms of all kinds.
The government intimated it could not
guarantee order within the state If
the Nazis were permitted to wear their
uniforms.

CHERBOURG, France, July 9
dN.SJ.-Although nearly every
one had given up hope that life
still existed aboard the sunken
submarine Promethee. the Italian
salvage ship Artiglio II arrived to-
day and Immediately prepared to
send divers down to make a final
check.


Despite dangerous currents and
a dense fog the Artiglio crew
planned to descend and attempt
to feed air lines to any compart-
ments free from water.


The plans were laid under the
most pessimistic circumstances,
however, as the time during which
any of the seamen could have lived
without more oxygen expired at
midnight last night.


The Artiglio, which recently sal
vaged millions of dollars in gold
bullion from the sunken liner
Egypt, was forced to await low
tide before it could send any men
down to the Promethee, believed
to lie 235 feet below the surface.

LOVINGTON, Ill, May 24.-Five bank
robbers spread terror through this town
for two hours early today They kid
naped the night watchman. wrecked the
Telephone Exchange, forced the cashier
of Hardware State Bank to open the
bank safe and escaped with s400.


Shortly after midnight they drove into
the village and pulled the night watch
man, Wilbur Redding, into their auto
mobile and drove away. They stopped
2 miles out of town and, exhibiting
three machine guns. told Redding they
would use them unless he did as they
instructed.


Forced to direct them to the home
Of Homer White. bank cashier, Redding
aroused White The robbers forced their
way into the house and, tying Mrs.
White with towels. they left a five-year-
old child sleeping and forced White and
his wife into the automobile.


At the telephone exchange they
aroused the operator, wrecked the
switchboard, tied the girl and put her In
their car. Both women were dragged
into the court house. where Boone
Dawson, night watchman. was tied up.


Proceeding to the bank, White was
forced to open two safes and hand over
the money. To make sure he was not
holding back funds, they examined the
cash book and departed without walt
ing for the time lock on the big vault.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, December 3.-With the
last Christmas merchandise ships clear
ing foreign ports today or tomorrow
and fleets Of liners laden with holiday
wares on the high seas bound for New
York, this port Is all set to handle the
biggest rush Of Yuletide imports since
1927.


These stacks Of imports, coming from
every nook and Granny of the globe, are
thoroughly inspected, valued and hur-
ried on to retailer as the appraisal force
here, which handles about rs per cent
of such work for the entire country,
tackles new cargoes arriving every few
hours.


This appraisal warehouse Is a good
place TO get a first-hand idea Of the
practical workings of foreign exchange,
for most imports passing through 1t
now come from countries whose cur
rency, In terms of American dollars Is
cheap. These include Great Britain,
Japan, Norway. Sweden, Spain, Den
mark, Yugoslayia, Czechoslovakta and
the South American countries.
Big Variety Inspected.


The twelfth floor Of the warehouse Is
symphony Of smells, as appraisers un-
wrap and examine foodstuffs. From
England come branded plum puddings,
mincemeat, fancy biscuits and cakes.
Norway, Sweden and Denmark send va
rious breads, anchovies and sardines.
France contributes goose hvers, glazed
fruits, walnuts and chocolates. Hol-
land sends cheese and cheese biscuits.
Italy and Spain offer olive oils, almonds
and chestnuts.


Odd shaped bottles from Germany
are filled with dealcoholized wines.
Spain sends diluted apple juice, Italy
many different non-alcoholic cordials
and vermouths.


China is sending fruit, loghan, vine
gar, bamboo shoots, eggs, peanuts,
sauces and various canned groceries, as
well as considerable ginger. Alongside
are cigars from Cuba and the Philip
pines, cigarettes from England and
Austria and tobacco from Turkey.
There are hills Of japanese goods,
! including various cheap mechanical
| toys, antimony ware made up into jew
elry and vanity boxes, vases, magnifying
glasses, sets of children's dishes, china
ware, silk ties, scarfs and wearing ap-
parel.


Foreign Gloves Handled.
In the drug department perfumes
from France mingle with other odors.
From nearby rooms come the smells Of
leather, as gloves from France, Ger
many, Belgium, Italy and Czechoslo-
vakia are handled.


In another section one finds lingerie
from France, table sets from Madeira,
linen bridge sets from Italy, linen hand
kerchiefs from Ireland, German artificial
flowers, knitted berets and scarfs from
Austria, silverware, diamonds, the latter
chiefly from Belgium; various kinds OF
jewelry, especially watches from Swift
zerland and paintings from Italy.

MEXICO CITY, March 2l.-Elever
Americans had arrived at their desti-
nations in Mexico safe. but late. today
after escaping from bandits who wreck
ed an international passenger train
yesterday near Mariscala, Queretaro
state.


The train carried three Pullman cars
from St. Louis and San Antonio. The
fireman and an express messenger were
killed, but soldiers, acting as train
escort, routed the bandits before they
could rob the passengers.


Oficials of the Mexican National
Railways today considered augmenting
train escorts. Soldiers secured the
hills above. Mariscala seeking the
bandits.


The wreck was caused by a rail which
the bandits had loosened and which the
train hit at normal speed.


Hardly had the dust settled when the
bandits, about 80 in number, closed in.
The detachment of soldiers was imme-
diately organized and drove back the
attackers, killing one of them.


In the checkup the conductor was
missing, but he soon appeared on an
engine from Mariscala with more SOL
diers. who joined in the pursuit.


The motive for the attack was sup
posed to have been robbery, although
former Provisional President Emilio
Portes Gil, on his way back to Mexico
from France, would have been aboard
the train had he continued direct to
Mexico City after leaving Laredo.


Among the Americans aboard the
train were J. D. McCarty and S. R.
Stenson, both of Chicago.

The two burglars who set the table
and dished the ice cream at sic Twelfth
street early yesterday lacked one domes-
tic virtue anyhow.


When Agnes Mustaugh opened her
restaurant for business she found a
table laid with two plates, two knives,
two forks, two empty ice cream dishes
and two spoons.


The unbidden guests had entered and
departed, carefully enough, by jimmy
ing a rear door. They had enjoyed a
repast of turkey and trimmings, topped
of with ice cream.


The ice cream container, the pro-
prietor was pleased to note, had been
scrupulously closed to prevent the rest
from melting.


Police, however, found possible iden-
tification marks in fingerprints on
sticky knives, plates and spoons.


The domestic pair had forgotten to
wash the dishes.

BY the Associated Press.


JACKSONVILLE, ILL.,, December 20.
-Tampering with switch was blamed
today by States Attorney Wolford H.
Absher as he investigated the wreck of
a Wabash passenger train that cost the
lives of two persons, injured two others
and endangered the lives of several
passengers.


The train swerved from the main line
Just inside the city limits last night,
shunted onto switch and crashed
into an oil tank car The engine and
one car overturned, drenched in a flood
of burning oil, which firemen quickly
extinguished.


The engineer, John Rapp, Springfield,
Ill, and H. L. Meyer, Decatur, ILL.,, died
from injuries Harry Ross, baggage
man from Jacksonville, was scalded,
and London Simmons, colored cook,
suffered a broken leg. The passengers
were shaken severely, but none was
hurt seriously.

The world today acclaims the
first woman ever to wing the
Atlantic in solo flight.


Five years ago today Charles
Augustus Lindbergh, an obscure
Midwesterner, successfully COM
pleted the first solo transatlantic
flight.


Today Amelia Earhsrt Putnam,
who bears a peculiar facial re-
semblance to that intrepid flier,
landed her plane at Londonderry,
Ireland.


This feat chalks up the second
transatlantic flight for the tall,
frail young woman, who four
years ago won worldwide fame
as the first woman successfully
to span the Atlantic.


Was Passenger Then


In that flight, however, Amelia
was accompanied by Pilot Wilmer
Stultz and Mechanic Lou Gordon.


The attention Of the world on
June 18, 1928, was focused on
the Friendship, a giant seaplane,
which took off from st. Johns,
Newfoundland, carrying the Bos-
ton settlement worker who
avowedly made the flight to laid
the family fortune"


After nine unsuccessful at
tempts to lift the huge Seaplane
into the air, it was off on that
dreary morning.


Overcast skies accompanied
that flight all the way to BURY
Inlet in South Wales and it was
a rain-Soaked multitude that
greeted the weary trio after its
2,400-mile flight.


First Woman Across


It was the first time a woman
had flown the Atlantic and it
was the first time that a sea
plane had accomplished a non
stop transatlantic flight.


Amelia had done it and with
cries of "Atta girl, Amelia" /"
London and Paris cheered the
woman who had made history.

And when she arrived in New
York, the ovation she received
was almost as loud and tumultu-
GUS as the acclaim given Indy.


But Mrs. Putnam, or just Miss
Earhart as she was then, isn't
famous only for her distance
flights.


The young woman also holds
the world speed record for wom-
en-, having flown 1877 miles an
hour.


Kept Romance Secret


Shy and reticent about most
everything, Miss Earhart kept a
curious nation completely in the
dark about her romance with the
backer of the famous flight of
Friendship, George Palmer Put
nam, well known New York pub
Usher.


But on February 8, 1881, it
leaked out that the famous flier
was wed to the publisher, whom
she had met for the first time
when the initial plans for the
flight were made.


While she was winging her way
across the Atlantic in 1928, how
ever, back home, Samuel Chap
man, a young man of Los
Angeles, was cheering her on. At
that time she was engaged to be
married to him,


Made AutOgirO Record


Not content with the accepted
type Of plane, Amelia bought her
self an autogiro last year and
accomplished the first coast-to-
coast autogiro flight.


This flight was a huge success,
except for one mishap. At Abb
lene, Tex, as she took off for the
last lap of the flight, her craft
crashed into two parked automo-
biles. But Amelia came out of
the wreckage smiling and un.
daunted.


She has accomplished many air
featS in a few years. What will
she do next?

HARRISONBURG, Va, July 8.-Run-
ming into a defective switch, Southern
Railway passenger train leaving Harri-
sonburg at $50 O'Clock this morning
was wrecked at Daphna and Engineer
Robert Good and Fireman Coon were
severely scalded by bursting steam pipes
Good and Coon were taken to the hos
pital at Harrisonburg, where it is stated
they will recover There were no pas
sengers on the train.


The engine and tender were turned
over on their sides. The combination
mail and two passenger coaches were
not overturned, though thrown from the
rails. The crossties for 200 feet we're
literally torn into splinters and the
heavy steel rails were twisted. The
heavy engine plowed through the road
bed for 100 feet. Two steel rails were
driven through the tender.


When the engine turned over on its
side the steam pipes were broken and
the whole countryside was awakened at
Daphna by the roar of escaping steam.

CHICAGO, December 19.-The over

improve the price of live stock within

vember 81, packers in the United States,

under the average for August to Sep
tember.


Restrictions on importations Of a
more permanent nature, to become ef-
fective after July /, 1888, have been
recommended by special parliament
ary commission which has been studying

United Kingdom for several months, "

tinued, in that the United Kingdom has
been the largest purchaser of American
pork products. The United States sup
plies more than three-fourths of the

swept into Georgia with diminished
force, leaving wreckage and scores of
injured. High winds whipped through

ant Grove

ground by the twisting wind. Wreck

ported at Chattanooga, Tenn, and

really know America until he has seen
its Capital

TRENTON, N. j., September IL
New Jersey Republicans are undergoing
the unpleasant experience this Fall OF
having their own weapons of past cam
Democratic organization, led by Frank
Hague, is working intensively to con-
vince the four-year voters, most Of them
commuters, that conditions will not get
better under the Hoover administration.


The Republican organization in past
presidential elections spread the doc
trine through large corporations, banks
and small business houses, that hard
times would follow if the Democrats
gained control. This propaganda was
peculiarly successful with the huge
North Jersey commuter vote, influenced
directly by New York City business con-
ditionS. And this four-year vote has
made the State consistently Republican
in presidential elections. although the
Democrats have elected four of the last
five Governors.


Mayor Hague and his organization are
concentrating on the dissatisfaction
among the white collar classes. Thirty
per cent of the commuters have lost
their jobs. Mayor Hague declared today
and another 30 have suffered drastic
salary reductions. These voters are the
same type that swung Maine for the
Democratic party, he said, and will
vote the Democratic ticket.


Leaders on both sides declare privately
the organization vote" will be far
less factor this year than in a long
time. The election will be dominated,
they say, by thousands of citizens who
have not bothered to vote when times
were good


This is the principal reason for the
confidence of the Democrats. 1t was a
resentment or protest vote that swept
Gov. Moore into office last November
and Mayor Hague has told his workers
the Maine election proves the same
sentiment is predominant still. The Re
publicans are hoping conditions will i'm
prove still further before election.
